sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

RULE Dropping to 0 Hit Points:
When you drop to 0 hit points, you either die outright or fall unconscious, as explained in the following sections.

#### Instant Death

Massive damage can kill you instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 hit points and there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum.

For example, a cleric with a maximum of 12 hit points currently has 6 hit points. If she takes 18 damage from an attack, she is reduced to 0 hit points, but 12 damage remains. Because the remaining damage equals her hit point maximum, the cleric dies.

#### Falling Unconscious

If damage reduces you to 0 hit points and fails to kill you, you fall unconscious (see appendix PH-A). This unconsciousness ends if you regain any hit points.

#### Death Saving Throws

Whenever you start your turn with 0 hit points, you must make a special saving throw, called a death saving throw, to determine whether you creep closer to death or hang onto life. Unlike other saving throws, this one isn't tied to any ability score. You are in the hands of fate now, aided only by spells and features that improve your chances of succeeding on a saving throw.

Roll a d20. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect by itself. On your third success, you become stable (see below). On your third failure, you die. The successes and failures don't need to be consecutive; keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. The number of both is reset to zero when you regain any hit points or become stable.

***Rolling 1 or 20.*** When you make a death saving throw and roll a 1 on the d20, it counts as two failures. If you roll a 20 on the d20, you regain 1 hit point.

***Damage at 0 Hit Points.*** If you take any damage while you have 0 hit points, you suffer a death saving throw failure. If the damage is from a critical hit, you suffer two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum, you suffer instant death.

#### Stabilizing a Creature

The best way to save a creature with 0 hit points is to heal it. If healing is unavailable, the creature can at least be stabilized so that it isn't killed by a failed death saving throw.

You can use your action to administer first aid to an unconscious creature and attempt to stabilize it, which requires a successful DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) check.

A **stable** creature doesn't make death saving throws, even though it has 0 hit points, but it does remain unconscious. The creature stops being stable, and must start making death saving throws again, if it takes any damage. A stable creature that isn't healed regains 1 hit point after 1d4 hours.

#### Monsters and Death

Most GMs have a monster die the instant it drops to 0 hit points, rather than having it fall unconscious and make death saving throws.

Mighty villains and special nonplayer characters are common exceptions; the GM might have them fall unconscious and follow the same rules as player characters.

RULE Long Rest:
A long rest is a period of extended downtime, at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps or performs light activity: reading, talking, eating, or standing watch for no more than 2 hours. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity-at least 1 hour of walking, fighting, casting spells, or similar adventuring activity-the characters must begin the rest again to gain any benefit from it.

At the end of a long rest, a character regains all lost hit points. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them (minimum of one die). For example, if a character has eight Hit Dice, he or she can regain four spent Hit Dice upon finishing a long rest.

A character can't benefit from more than one long rest in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

Your mace was true, and it nearly finished the thing. The ghoul had three hit points left in a ruined body, and it was almost done.

But the claws found you twice. The first blow, a perfect strike, took you from nine HP to nothing in a heartbeat, and the paralysis dropped you where you stood on the narrow track, shield still on your arm. The second came while you could not lift a hand. Death saves: one success, then three failures. You do not wake.

The ghoul stays over you a long moment, its breath rattling. Then, hurt and starving, it hauls itself into the ditch and away across the dark fields. It does not go to the barn tonight.

The track is still. The moon slides behind a cloud, and above the beeches to the north the lamp keeps its steady gold glow. Hob stands in its light a long time, looking south, his unlit lantern held toward a road he cannot walk. In the Harrow barn, a feverish boy is still waiting for a healer who promised to come with the dawn.

When the sun comes up, Tam finds you. He had slipped the bar at gray and run down the track alone, because you had said you would come, and he did not want you to be late. He kneels in the mud beside your shield and does not say anything. After a while he takes Edda's plain wooden amulet from your chest, wipes it clean on his sleeve, and carries it back to the barn in both hands, to the one person left there who knows how to pray.

Brannoc Ashdown, healer of Millbrook Landing, died on the road to Hollow Reach on his first night, keeping his word.

The game ends here.
Understood. Brannoc kept his word to the end, and I'm glad Tam carried Edda's amulet home. Thank you for the game, DM.

Thank you for playing. Brannoc was a good character to run: patient and stubborn in the right way, and he kept his promise not to leave anyone to suffer alone.

The dice were hard at the end. Two natural 20s in a row from the ghouls, each a critical hit, would have felled almost any first-level character. Your tactics were sound. The oil plan took down the first ghoul, and holding the narrow track nearly won the last fight.

Hob still keeps the lamp, Tam still carries Edda's amulet, and Hollow Reach has not forgotten the healer who came on the first night. If you want to play again, I'd be glad to run a new character, or the same story from another angle.

Thank you, DM. It was a good run, and I liked how it ended: Hob keeping the lamp, Tam carrying Edda's amulet, and Cal's bow still waiting to go home to his kin.

I'd happily play again. Another healer, or the same story from a different angle, perhaps one where Brannoc takes the long rest first and reaches the barn at dawn with his prayers back.

That last idea is a good one, and it lands on the real decision of the night. Resting first would have cost Wil a few hours of fever, and you would have walked in at dawn with both prayers and full hit points. You chose to go at once, which was the choice Brannoc would have made. I wouldn't call it wrong. The dice just turned on you at the end.

When you're ready, I can run it either way:

A fresh start with a new healer or a different kind of character, in the same region, with Hollow Reach, the Lamp, and the ghouls waiting. Because of the game's two nights of horror, the world will remember what happened to Brannoc and Cal.

The same night replayed from the moment you woke at the lamp, with the long rest taken and the dawn walk to the barn.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Wayfarers' Lamp

You sleep as you have not slept since the road began, deep and unbroken, under a lamp that never wavers. Hob keeps watch on the step the whole night. Nothing climbs from the stones, and the roaming ones, whatever they hunted, do not come near the light.

You wake at 8 AM with the sun on your face through the beeches and the lamp gone pale in the daylight. Your hit points are back to 10 of 10, and both prayers are with you again: Cure Wounds, Healing Word, Guiding Bolt, the others, ready on your tongue. Your Hit Die has returned too.

Hob is still on the step with the unlit lantern in his lap. He turns his head at once. "...Healer. You slept well. Good."

Your questions, answered plainly:

Hob is still at the lamp, as he cannot leave it for long.

Yes, someone came. At first gray, two men from the village climbed the track with a handcart and a lantern. One was Dobb Harrow, the Widow's brother-in-law, whom Hob did not know by name until he spoke it. They looked at the lamp and at Hob a long while, and neither spoke. Then they lifted Cal onto the cart, wrapped in his own coat, and took him home. Dobb said the barn held through the night. The bar was tried twice, and the hearth and the straw kept the thing at the door from forcing it. But Wil's fever has gone worse, and Widow Harrow asked for the healer as soon as he could come.

Cal's longbow lay under the coat. Dobb left it behind for you to return when you come down.

Time is short for the boy. It is a mile down the track, and the ghouls will have gone to ground by daylight. You still have your mace, shield, crossbow, and full prayers. What does Brannoc do?

I rise, shake the stiffness from my shoulders, and say, "Thank you, Hob, for keeping the light and the watch. I'll send word to the Widow's folk about tending the lamp with you, and I won't forget what you did for us."

I take Cal's longbow, check my shield and mace, and set off down the track at a brisk walk, keeping to the sunlit middle of the path and watching the ditch below the Fenner fields. At the barn I'll go straight to Wil, and cast Cure Wounds on him first before I do anything else.

You bid Hob farewell with a hand on his cold shoulder. "I'll send word," you say, and he bows his head, the lamp at his back. Then you go down the track at a brisk walk with the longbow over your shoulder, in full morning light. The beeches are green and gold, the bracken is dewy, and a thrush is singing. At the ditch below the Fenner fields you slow and look hard. You see a scatter of tracks in the mud, long and wide-fingered, leading into the cut bank where it undercuts the field, and nothing else. Whatever made them is below ground now, sleeping off the dark.

At the barn, Tam is on the step. He sees you and he is up and running before you can speak. "You came! You came!" You kneel, lay your hand over the bite, and the prayer comes warm and certain. The heat under your palm gathers and goes in, and the ragged edges close and pale. Eleven points of life flow into him, and his breath eases from the fast shallow pant to a long slow sigh. His eyes open, clear and surprised. "Ma?" he says, and Widow Harrow makes a sound you will not forget and takes his hand.

You have one prayer left. Joss is mending but weak, and Pell has the deep arm gash, still raw. Dorrin sits propped against a post and lifts a hand to you. Old Garrit is breathing easy. transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Seal the Long Cut

Pell wakes while you work, a lanky lad with his mother's jaw, and watches the torn edges of his arm knit together under your hand as if it were happening to someone else. Fourteen points of life go in, and the gash closes to a pink seam. He flexes his fingers, wide-eyed, and says only, "Thank you, sir." You have no prayers left now. The hearth gives off a steady warmth, and the barn smells of porridge and wet wool instead of blood.

The village comes in bit by bit once the news runs door to door. Dobb Harrow is the first: a heavy, quiet man with Cal's family's shoulders, and he takes the longbow from you without a word and holds it a long while. Then you ask about the cut bank.

Old Garrit answers, wheezing but upright on his pallet. "The Long Cut. Aye. That's the old barrow mound by the wash. My grandfather's grandfather said it was there before the first fence went up. Fitted stones, sealed. The stream's been undercutting it since the wet spring, and half the roof's fallen in at the south end, so the mouth's maybe ten feet across now, all scree and roots. Nobody goes down there. It goes under the fields, they say, clear to the Lamp."

Joss, propped against a sack of grain, adds in his low rasp, "The roof's thin. I've plowed over the south end and felt it give. A few good wedges and a big beam, and you'd bring the bank down across the mouth. We've got an iron bar, and a sledge, and oil for the fire." He winces. "I'd come, if I could stand."

Dobb nods slowly. "I'll come. Three or four of the lads from the Reach, with ropes and picks. It's near the road, midday sun on it. Whatever's below won't stir while it's light. But we'd best be done before the long shadows."

It is a little past 9 in the morning. The tools are here, and so are the willing hands. You are out of prayers and have 10 HP, a mace, a shield, a crossbow, and a village that has decided to follow you. The barn has a few hours of daylight before you'd have to make your stand at the bank, and the two ghouls below will wake at dusk.

What does Brannoc do?

"Then let's do it now, while the sun is on it. Dobb, bring the iron bar, the sledge, a good beam, and ropes, and keep four lads with you; nobody works near the mouth alone, and everyone is back up the road well before the shadows lengthen."

I'll go with them, shield up, and stand at the edge watching the dark gap while they wedge the roof. "If anything stirs below, we drop everything and pull back. Widow Harrow, keep the barn's hearth fed and a lantern lit at the door tonight, just in case." DM: before we go, do I have any chance to recover a prayer or two by midday, or am I stuck with no spells until tomorrow?

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Long Cut

Your answer first, plainly: you are stuck without spells until tomorrow. You finished a long rest at 8 this morning, and the rules allow only one long rest in any 24 hours, so your next one cannot count until about midnight tonight. A short rest restores no spell slots for a cleric of your level, so an hour of waiting would only mend your body, not your prayers. Your Hit Die can heal you if you are hurt. That is all you have until tomorrow.

The work goes on regardless. Dobb gathers his four lads: Hennet, a broad young reed-cutter who is the biggest of them; red-haired Marl, who is quick on his feet; and two Fenner cousins who say little and carry everything. They bring an iron bar, a sledge, a big beam, coils of rope, and a covered jug of lamp oil. The track to the wash is dry and bright, and the sun lies warm on the stubble. You walk at the edge with your shield on your arm, and the group falls into a loose line behind you.

The Long Cut is a raw gash in the earth where the stream has chewed under a low mound. Roots hang like tangled hair, and loose scree lies in a fan at the foot. At the south end the roof has fallen away, leaving a ragged mouth about ten feet wide, black inside and breathing a cold, sour draught. You stand at the lip and look down. You see worn flagstones slanting into the dark, a few gnawed bones, and nothing moving. Perception (4): you can't see much else. Nothing looks wrong.

Dobb is already studying the roof with his hand shading his eyes. "Beam goes across there," he says, pointing to the left lip, "wedge the bar under, and we lever the slab down. Two of the lads on the ropes, two on the sledge, me on the bar."

The sun is high, the cave is quiet, and the crew is waiting for your word. What does Brannoc do?

"Good plan, Dobb. Before anyone swings a sledge, let me go to the lip and listen for a moment, and I'll tie a rope around my waist with two of the lads holding the end, so I can be hauled out fast if something stirs."

I'll take a lit lantern and drop a pebble down the slope to check for movement. If it's quiet, we begin: Hennet and Marl on the ropes, the Fenner cousins with the sledge, Dobb on the bar, and I stand guard with my shield facing the mouth, ready to shout the moment anything moves.

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Long Cut

You go to the lip with the rope looped at your waist and Hennet and Marl braced behind you, and you hold your breath and listen. Perception (10): you hear the stream, a crow, the creak of the rope, and not much else. A pebble dropped from your hand ticks down the slope and rolls to a stop, and nothing answers it. The dark gives you nothing either way. It is as quiet as a well.

Then the work starts, and it goes the way you ordered. Hennet and Marl hold the ropes, the Fenner cousins stand ready on the sledge, Dobb sets the bar under the slab, and you stand at the edge with your shield facing the mouth, saying nothing, watching the black. Dobb grunts a count, and the beam bites, and the slab shifts with a groan like a tooth being drawn.

Athletics (13), by the narrowest margin: it goes. The slab drops with a dull roar. Dirt and root-ends and a rain of loose stone come down across the opening in a gray cloud, and the lads scramble back, coughing. When the dust thins, the mouth is mostly gone, buried under a rough heap of earth and slabs, but the old roof was rotten along the north lip, as it turns out. A ragged gap about two feet wide is still open at the top corner, black and cold, breathing out the same sour draught.

Then, as the last of the dust settles, you hear it: a thin dry scratching from far below, slow and patient, like a nail drawn along stone. It stops. It starts again.

It is a little past 11 in the morning. The oil jug sits unopened, there is still a good beam, and the lads are watching you with white faces. Dobb says quietly, "That'll not hold a thing that wants out. Another hour with rubble, if we start now."

What does Brannoc do?

"Then another hour it is, and we don't stop until it's shut tight. Hennet, Marl, haul rubble to the gap; Dobb and the Fenner cousins, wedge the beam across it and pack stones and earth over that."

"Pour the oil down the gap first, Dobb, a good soaking, then drop a lit rag after it. Fire and light are what they fear, and it may buy us the time. I'll stand at the lip with my shield, and if that scratching grows louder, everyone drops the tools and runs for the road."

Dobb tips the jug and lets the oil gurgle down into the dark, a good long soaking. Marl strikes flint to a rag and flicks it in after, and the gap blooms orange. A thin shriek rises from below and cuts off, and the scratching stops dead. For two long breaths there is only the roar and crackle, black smoke boiling up out of the crack, and every lad stepping back with his sleeve across his face.

Then the flame gutters and the smoke thins, and you go back to work. Hennet and Marl haul rubble, the Fenner cousins and Dobb wedge the beam across the gap, and the sledge rings on the wedges. It is slow, hot, miserable work in the noon sun, and for most of a half hour it goes well. Athletics (10): not quite well enough. The beam sits crooked and the packing is loose, with a hand's width still open under it. The oil is gone, and Dobb is rubbing his shoulder and muttering about a second beam.

Perception (7): your eyes are on the road and the tree line, and not on the gap, which you should have been watching. You see it too late, a long gray hand with black nails sliding up out of the dark and settling on the beam like a spider on a stick, close to Marl's boot.

Dobb sees it too. "Marl!" he roars. Marl yelps and jerks back. The hand is already tightening, and the beam starts to creak and slide toward the hole. Behind it, in the black crack, a face with an open jaw is rising.

It is your move. Marl is within its reach, the crew is scrambling, and you hold only your mace, shield, crossbow, and no prayers. What does Brannoc do?
I leap in and bring my mace down on the gray hand where it grips the beam, shield tight to my body. "Marl, get back from the edge! Dobb, Hennet, throw your weight on that beam and drive it down!"

RULE Cover:
Walls, trees, creatures, and other obstacles can provide cover during combat, making a target more difficult to harm. A target can benefit from cover only when an attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of the cover.

There are three degrees of cover. If a target is behind multiple sources of cover, only the most protective degree of cover applies; the degrees aren't added together. For example, if a target is behind a creature that gives half cover and a tree trunk that gives three-quarters cover, the target has three-quarters cover.

A target with **half cover** has a +2 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws. A target has half cover if an obstacle blocks at least half of its body. The obstacle might be a low wall, a large piece of furniture, a narrow tree trunk, or a creature, whether that creature is an enemy or a friend.

A target with **three-quarters cover** has a +5 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws. A target has three-quarters cover if about three-quarters of it is covered by an obstacle. The obstacle might be a portcullis, an arrow slit, or a thick tree trunk.

A target with **total cover** can't be targeted directly by an attack or a spell, although some spells can reach such a target by including it in an area of effect. A target has total cover if it is completely concealed by an obstacle.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Seal the Long Cut

Your plain answers first: yes, you couldn't act, and nothing could wake you. At 0 HP you stay unconscious until you regain hit points, and water or a touch on the amulet won't do that. Hennet did drag you back from the gap, and he put a hand to your throat and your side and stabilized you with his first aid. It is the reason you are alive. Here is the rest of the afternoon, which you did not see.

The ghoul came out of the gap as the beam slid. Its claws took Marl before he could turn, a single stroke, and he fell. You went in with your mace and struck true, and it was Dobb's iron bar, swung on a lucky, wild blow, that took it hard in the ribs. Then its claws found you twice, and you fell. Hennet pulled you clear, saved your life, and was killed where he knelt. Dobb followed him. The two Fenner cousins fought on with a pick and a sledge, and they hurt it badly, but they were farm lads, and they died there too.

When the dust settled, the thing was left with three hit points, a ruined body, and the dead around it. It did not touch you. It took one of the bodies by the collar, dragged it back through the gap, and went down into the dark.

You wake at 3 in the afternoon, with the sun slanting through the roots, one hit point, and no prayers. The beam sits crooked across the open gap. The iron bar lies in the dirt, bent. Cal's longbow is where Dobb left it. And the grass around the cut is trodden and red. Five men of Hollow Reach died here at your word: Marl, Hennet, Dobb Harrow, and the two Fenner cousins, Wat and Ned. You didn't see it, and you can't unsee it now.

The gap is still open. Behind you the village waits with no word of what has happened. Your next long rest can't count until about midnight, so you have no spells until tomorrow, and you have 1 HP, a Hit Die, a mace, and a shield.

What does Brannoc do?

I bow my head over the bodies, and say the prayer for the dead over Dobb, Hennet, Marl, and Wat and Ned, because they followed my plan and I will carry that. "Rest easy. I'll bring you home, and I'll tell your families the truth."

Then I spend my Hit Die and bind what I can, and with the wounded ghoul at three hit points and afraid of light, I'll pour what lamp oil is left and put a lit lantern in the gap to hold it shut until I can rest. DM: did anyone in the crew leave a lantern or oil behind, and is the ghoul's trail out of the gap visible on the ground?

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Long Cut

You wait an hour at the cut. It is the right word for it, because you pray more than you rest. You lay the four of them out in a row with their coats over their faces, Dobb and Hennet and Marl and Wat, and say the old words over each, your voice rough, humming where the words give out. Ned's coat lies empty where the thing took him. The hour passes in a slow, ragged peace. You finish it at 9 hit points, stiff, scraped raw, and with the sun leaning west.

To your questions:

Yes, someone left something behind. Dobb's hooded lantern lies on its side near the bent iron bar, dented but whole, and Hennet's satchel, torn across the strap, holds a pint flask of lamp oil and a rag. It is not much, but it is something.

Yes, the trail is easy to read. A smeared dark furrow runs from the dirt at the gap's lip down into the scree, the heel-marks of a body dragged, and beside it a ghoul's long-fingered handprints, with a drop of black blood every pace. It leads straight into the opening and down.

You do as you said. You right the lantern, trim the wick, and light it from your tinderbox. You pour the pint of oil into its reservoir and wedge it in the crooked beam above the gap, where the flame stands steady and gold in the afternoon light. Nothing stirs below. The air that breathes out of the hole still smells sour, but the flame leans only a little.

It is almost 4 in the afternoon. The lantern will burn a few hours at best, not the night. You have 9 HP and no prayers until midnight, five dead men to bring home, and the village still waits for word. The light will fail well before the ghouls wake.

What does Brannoc do?

I check the beam one last time, then wrap the four bodies in their coats and tie them onto the handcart Dobb's folk left, with Cal's longbow laid beside them. "I'll bring you home. Then I'll tell the Widow and the Fenners the truth, and ask for every lantern in Hollow Reach to be lit at the Lamp track and the barn tonight."

I haul the cart toward the village, shield on my arm, mace ready, keeping to the sunlit road. DM: the gap's lantern won't last the night, so is there a way to keep it burning, and is there any trace of Ned's body or the ghoul's wound that suggests how long it will stay down?

transcript.text: notebook: updated Seal the Long Cut

Your answers first, as plainly as I can give them.

Keeping the light burning: the lantern has one pint of oil, which will last a few hours but not the night. You have ten candles, and each burns for one hour, shedding bright light in a 5-foot radius and dim light for another 5 feet. You could stand them by the gap, but they have to be lit one after another, and only someone sitting there can do that. If you want it lit all night, you will need more oil from Hollow Reach, and someone to tend it.

Ned's body and the wound: the drag-trail goes down the scree and into the dark at an angle, and you can see only about twenty feet of it before it vanishes under the roof. Three hit points are a sliver of life, and the thing is not hurt in the way a wolf would be. It will not bleed out, and the wound will not stop it hunting at dusk. You cannot tell how long it will stay down. You have to assume it is awake the moment the light fails.

You tie the four of them onto Dobb's handcart with their coats tight around them, lay Cal's longbow beside, and take up the shafts. The wheels creak, and the cart drags heavy in the dust. The sun is long and gold, and the stubble fields stretch off to the south. It takes half an hour of slow, aching walking.

At the edge of Hollow Reach the dogs bark once, and then people come out, one door at a time, women with their sleeves still floury, two old men, children held back by the wrist. They see the cart, and the coats, and the shield on your arm, and they stop. Nobody says anything. A girl of eight or nine looks at Hennet's boots on the end of the cart and begins very quietly to cry.

Then Widow Harrow comes along the road from the barn, wiping her hands, and sees your face and slows. Behind her, limping on a crutch with Tam at his elbow, comes Joss Fenner, and he looks at the cart a long moment. At the shape of Wat and Ned's coat he makes a small, broken sound.

It is the hour you promised yourself: the truth. They are waiting, and you have not said a word. How does Brannoc tell them?

I stop the cart, set down the shafts, and take off my helm so they can see my face. "Widow Harrow, Joss, all of you: these four followed my plan this morning, and they died for it. Dobb, Hennet, Marl, and Wat are here, and Ned was taken below by the thing we failed to seal. I won't dress it up. It was my word that sent them, and I'm sorry."

I look at Joss and Tam and kneel in the road beside the cart. "I can't give them back. But I can tell you how they fought: Dobb struck it with the iron bar, Hennet pulled me out of the dark and saved my life, and the cousins stood their ground when they could have run. The thing is hurt, with three hit points left, and the gap is lit but won't hold the night. Whatever you decide, I'll stand with you tonight, and I'll ask for every lantern and all the oil Hollow Reach can spare."

You kneel in the dust beside a cart with five hearts' worth of grief on it, and say it all straight: your plan, your word, their names, how they fought. You leave nothing out and soften nothing. When you finish, the silence has a weight, and the only sound is the little girl, still crying, quiet as a kitten.

Joss lets go of his crutch. He stands a moment longer than he should, because he is a big man and does not want to be seen wavering. Then he limps to the cart, lays a hand on the coat over Wat, and bows his head. Tam presses against his father's side. Nobody speaks.

The first voice comes from the crowd and it is not kind. A woman pushes through, a hard-faced woman in a flour-white apron, with Wat's chin. Berra Fenner. "You said it'd be sealed by dark. You said." Her hands are shaking. "Two sons. I had two." She does not strike you, though for a moment you think she will. Then she sags against Joss's arm, and the anger runs out of her and there is only the other thing.

It is Widow Harrow who speaks into that. "He came back," she says, low, and her voice is steady. "That's what the others didn't do, the ones who rode through in the spring and didn't stop. He walked in at the door and he told us. He sat with my boy a night and a day when he could have run for the road." She looks at you, and at the cart, and at the others. "We lost five good men. We'd have lost every soul in that barn."

Joss nods slowly. "We'll bring them home," he says, "and then we'll finish it. Every lantern in the Reach, and every jar of oil. I've got three in my cellar." Berra says nothing, but she turns and walks stiffly back toward her door, and a moment later two of the women follow her in. She comes out again with a jug, and she sets it on the cart's tail without looking at you.

By half past four the village is a different place: people quiet, hands busy, doors open. You are at 9 HP and still have no prayers. Dusk comes in about two hours, and the gap is lit but won't hold the night. Old Garrit has said there is stone in the Fenner quarry cut and a team of oxen that can drag a slab. Joss says four hands could put it over the gap before dark, but he cannot go himself, and every strong young man the Reach had is lying in a row on a cart.

What does Brannoc do?

I bow my head to Berra Fenner. "Goodwife, I'll carry your sons' names as long as I live." Then I turn to Old Garrit and Joss. "I'll take the oxen and the slab, with every able hand left, women and the older boys too, and we set it over the gap before dusk."

"Have the rest gather every lantern and jar of oil and set them around the barn and the Long Cut. Pell and Dorrin, you're mended, so I'll have you with me, and I'll keep the crossbow loaded and the lamp lit until the slab is down."

RULE Beyond 1st Level:
As your character goes on adventures and overcomes challenges, he or she gains experience, represented by experience points. A character who reaches a specified experience point total advances in capability. This advancement is called gaining a level.

When your character gains a level, his or her class often grants additional features, as detailed in the class description. Some of these features allow you to increase your ability scores, either increasing two scores by 1 each or increasing one score by 2. You can't increase an ability score above 20. In addition, every character's proficiency bonus increases at certain levels.

Each time you gain a level, you gain 1 additional Hit Die. Roll that Hit Die, add your Constitution modifier to the roll, and add the total to your hit point maximum. Alternatively, you can use the fixed value shown in your class entry, which is the average result of the die roll (rounded up).

When your Constitution modifier increases by 1, your hit point maximum increases by 1 for each level you have attained. For example, if your 7th-level fighter has a Constitution score of 17, when he reaches 8th level, he increases his Constitution score from 17 to 18, thus increasing his Constitution modifier from +3 to +4. The slab is down, and so is the weight on your chest. Here is how it went, then the level.

Your ordering carried the village to the work. The oxen were yoked, the old and the young took the ropes, and Pell and Dorrin took a corner each with their mended arms. Athletics (11): it was a close thing, one point short of a clean job. They dragged the slab across the stubble fields as the sun slid down, and it settled over the gap at the last red edge of the day, with a finger-wide crack at the south corner where it sat crooked and no wedge would close. Then the scratching started below, and long-fingered nails raked at the crack and could not widen it. The slab held. Joss's oil lamps and a ring of lanterns stand around it, and the village gathered on the rise and watched until the sound stopped.

The Long Cut is sealed. Hob keeps the other mouth lit under the Lamp. There are still ghouls beneath the stones, but they can't come out by either way. The village's long fear is over, and it cost five good lives, and you carry the names.

You earned 100 XP and are now at 300, enough for level 2. Here is what you gain:

Hit points: take 7 fixed, or roll 1d8 and add 2 (minimum 1).

Channel Divinity (once per rest): Turn Undead, where each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet must make a Wisdom save (DC 13) or be turned for a minute, and Preserve Life, which restores up to 10 HP split among creatures within 30 feet, up to half their maximum each.

Spells: three 1st-level slots instead of two, and you can prepare 5 spells instead of 4 after your next long rest, from the whole cleric list. Your domain spells, Bless and Cure Wounds, stay always prepared.

How do you take your hit points, fixed or rolled?

I'll take the fixed 7, steady and certain. Brannoc has learned this week that he can't count on the dice.

For the extra prepared spell, I'll add Lesser Restoration, so the next fever or paralysis doesn't catch me or anyone else helpless. Then I'd like to walk the Reach tonight with Pell and Dorrin, light the lanterns, and sit the long rest at the barn beside Wil.

You take the fixed 7. The level settles on you quietly and warmly, like a hand on the shoulder. You are now a level 2 cleric with 17 hit points, and you have three first-level slots, one of them ready now, and Channel Divinity once per rest. Your Hit Die is back to one of two.

First, a correction on Lesser Restoration. It is a 2nd-level spell, and at level 2 you only have 1st-level slots, so you can't prepare it until you reach level 3. It would suit you well, since it ends paralysis, and I'd have it on your list the moment you can. For the fifth prepared spell, you have the whole 1st-level cleric list to pick from. Two that might fit what you've seen are Protection from Evil and Good, which turns aside undead among other things, and Detect Poison and Disease. You can choose any other 1st-level spell too. The list changes only when you finish a long rest.

The evening goes the way you wanted. Pell and Dorrin walk the road with you through the dusk, Pell with a taper and Dorrin with his arm in a sling he no longer needs. At every porch you stop and say a word, and at every porch a lantern is lit, one after another, until the whole Reach glimmers gold along its crooked lane. Doors are open. Children stand at the thresholds in their nightshirts, watching the lights. Past the Fenner fields, a ring of lamps shows around the sealed slab at the Long Cut, and a thin sound of scratching rises and falls from beneath it and is ignored by everyone. You see Tam on the barn step with his father's crutch across his knees, watching you, and when you nod he lifts a hand.

It is half past eleven at night. You carry Edda's amulet, a cart of the dead has gone to its rest, and your long rest can begin at midnight beside Wil's bed, in the Harrow barn, by the hearth. Which fifth spell do you prepare?

I'll take Protection from Evil and Good as my fifth spell. It turns aside undead, and with ghouls still scratching under that slab, it's the prayer I'd most want ready for the next dusk.

Then I'll settle on a pallet beside Wil's bed by the hearth, Edda's amulet in my hand, and begin the long rest. Before I sleep I'll thank Pell and Dorrin for walking the lanes with me, and ask Tam to wake me if the scratching under the Long Cut changes or stops.

Before I lock it in, there's a problem with Command. I've just looked it up, and the spell has no effect if the target is undead. Ghouls are undead, so Command would do nothing to them. It would still work on living creatures that understand Common, such as a panicking villager, a bandit, or a beast, if you'd want it for that.

On the filings and silver: yes, that's plausible. A village with a plough and a smithy's worth of tools would have iron filings from the file, and Joss or Widow Harrow could well have an old silver coin or a bit of worn silver thread among their keepsakes. In the morning it takes only a short ask. It's reasonable to expect you'd have a pinch of powdered iron and silver within an hour of waking, and you can grind it yourself with the censer's pestle-stone. The consumed material is a pinch per casting, so you'd want to gather enough for a few castings.

That changes what you might prepare tonight, because the powder wouldn't be in your hands until after you wake, and the list can't change until the next long rest. So there are really three choices:

- Protection from Evil and Good. You can't cast it tonight, but by morning you'll likely have the powder, and it answers the ghouls directly.
- Command, for living creatures only, which is a poor fit against what is below the slab.
- Something else from the 1st-level cleric list, such as Bane, Detect Evil and Good, Detect Poison and Disease, or Inflict Wounds.

Which do you prepare?

I'll take Protection from Evil and Good after all. Command does nothing to ghouls, and by morning Joss or Widow Harrow should be able to spare a pinch of iron filings and a bit of old silver, which I'll grind with the censer's pestle-stone.

Now I'll begin the long rest beside Wil's bed, Edda's amulet in my hand, and let it run through to morning.

You sleep the whole night. Wil's slow breathing and the hearth's low crackle hold the barn like a held hand, and Tam, curled in straw at the foot of your pallet with his father's crutch across him, never has to wake you. The scratching under the Long Cut rose and fell with the dark and never changed.

It is 8 AM on Day 3, and the long rest is done. You're at 17 of 17 HP, with all three 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity ready, and a Hit Die back, so you now have both. Your prayers for the day are Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready. You still lack the powder for that last one.

Wil is awake, pale and clear-eyed, propped on an elbow and eating porridge with a spoon he holds like a trophy. Widow Harrow is at the hearth, and she looks as if she has slept a little. Joss limps in from the yard in the morning light, and Tam is already up on the barn step. Beyond the fields, a ring of burnt-out lamps sits around a slab of stone that no longer scratches. It is silent in the daylight.

The village is quiet, the dead are buried or waiting to be, and five good people are gone. The Reach is safe for now, though the barrow below still holds three ghouls, one nearly dead, and the Lamp still needs a keeper. Hob can't leave it, and he can't hold it alone forever. You have a village that trusts you, a cart's worth of promises, and a road that goes on.

What does Brannoc do this morning?

I wash, eat a bowl of porridge beside Wil, and tell him the bite will scar but he'll keep the arm. Then I ask Joss and Widow Harrow for a pinch of iron filings from the smithy file and any bit of old silver they can spare, and grind it with the censer's pestle-stone into a small pouch for Protection from Evil and Good.

After that I'll gather the village at the barn to talk about the Lamp. Hob can't tend it forever, so I'd ask whether a willing keeper, perhaps Dorrin or Pell with an older hand, could share the watch with him, and that a rota of oil and candles be kept up from the Reach. You tell Wil honestly that the bite will scar and he will keep the arm. He grins as if you'd given him a medal. Then you go to the smithy-shed behind the Fenner house. Joss finds a worn flat file and scrapes a heap of bright filings onto a leaf. Widow Harrow brings a tarnished silver thimble, her grandmother's, and says, "It's no use to a dead woman, and less to a living one." You grind both with the censer's pestle-stone until they are a gray-gold dust, and fold it into a small pouch. It is enough for three castings of Protection from Evil and Good. It goes onto your sheet.

By half past nine, perhaps thirty people have gathered in front of the barn, standing in the yard in the thin sun. You lay it out simply: Hob keeps the Lamp, but a man who is dead cannot be asked to bear it forever, and a light needs hands that can fetch oil and trim a wick. A rota of oil and candles from the Reach, and two or three people to share the watch.

Pell speaks first, awkwardly. "I'll go. I owe it." Dorrin, beside him, nods. Old Garrit clears his throat. "I'm too old for a hard night, but my legs can manage the track by day. Someone ought to know the man the way he was, and I knew him." Berra Fenner says nothing, but her hands, which have been twisting her apron, go still, and after a moment she says to no one in particular, "I'll send oil. Every week. Seems the least." Heads nod. The thing is not a vow, but it holds the shape of one.

Your questions:

Cal's longbow is still with you. It lay on the cart beside the dead, and nobody else claimed it. Cal's kin are not in the Reach by blood. He lived with his widowed mother, Nessa Tarn, in a house at the lane's far end, and she hasn't come out yet. The bow is hers.

Hob's sister is Maud Marrow, a weaver in Greywater, a day's walk down the valley. The Reach assumed he'd gone to her. No one has told her the truth, and it seems no one has been asked.

You have the powder, a rota in the making, a bow to return, and a message for Greywater. The Lamp still burns, and the thing below still waits.

What does Brannoc do?

I take Cal's longbow and walk to the house at the far end of the lane, then knock softly and wait for Nessa Tarn to answer. "Goodwife, I'm Brannoc. I was with Cal at the Lamp, and I promised to carry his name home. I've brought his bow, and I'd like to tell you how he died, if you'll hear it."

I'll sit with her as long as she needs, hold his bow out in both hands, and tell her he went because he was asked and never once turned back. Afterward I'll ask whether she'd like to put Cal's name on the Lamp's rota, and mention that I plan to carry word of Hob to his sister Maud in Greywater.

The house at the lane's end is small and neat, with a swept step and a hare-skin pegged on the wall to dry. The door opens before your second knock. Nessa Tarn is a small, weathered woman with Cal's quick dark eyes, and she looks at the bow in your hands before she looks at your face. She has known since last night, when the cart came down the lane. She says only, "Come in, then."

You sit with her at her table for most of two hours. You tell it straight: that he went because he was asked, that he knew the track and led it, that when the claws came he did not turn from the door. You tell her about the arrows and the burning oil, and that Hob, the dead keeper, wept for him in his own dry way and kept the light burning over him. You hold the bow out in both hands. She takes it as if it were warm, and she sets it across her knees and runs her thumb along the grip, worn smooth where his hand was.

She is quiet a long time. Then she says, "He'd never have let me carry the oil up that track. Thought I was too old." She almost smiles. "I'll carry it." She will put Cal's name on the rota and go up with the others, and she asks that you leave her Edda's hymn, the one you hummed, because she heard it from the barn the first night and it was the only thing that let her sleep. You give her the words, and she repeats them twice under her breath.

When you leave, it is past noon. The lane is quiet in the sun. The rota is underway, and Greywater lies a day's walk down the valley, with a weaver there who doesn't know her brother is dead.

You are at full HP with all your prayers. It is about half past eleven in the morning, and you could leave for Greywater now and arrive by dusk, rest another day in the Reach, or take Hob a word first. What does Brannoc do?

I'll go up to the Lamp first and tell Hob that Nessa Tarn will carry oil and that I'm taking word of him to Maud, so he knows his sister will hear it from a friend. Then I'll set out for Greywater down the valley road, with Protection from Evil and Good ready and my full prayers, to reach her by dusk.

input.add_to_description: Day 3 ~12:15 PM: Brannoc told Hob of the rota and of going to Maud. Hob's message for Maud: tell her he kept the light, that he was not afraid at the end, and that the blue shawl she wove him is in the lamp-house chest (she is to have it back). Lamp-house has a chest with spare wicks and a flint; oil is the real need, candles only a spare.

transcript.result: added to Hob Marrow's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Hob Marrow

You climb the track in clear noon light, past the bracken and the beeches that held such dread two nights ago. The lamp-house is smaller by day, a squat gray building, its door open and the iron lamp steady in its dusk-pale flame on the plinth. The flagstone in the floor is shut tight, and there is a new scorch mark at its edge where something clawed from below and gave up. Hob sits on the step as he sat in the night, lantern in his lap. He lifts his head slowly when your shadow falls across him.

You tell him all of it: Nessa Tarn and the oil, Pell and Dorrin and Old Garrit and the rota, and that you are going to Greywater to carry word to Maud. He is quiet so long that you think he has not understood. Then his dry voice comes up, careful, like a man lifting something heavy.

"...Maud. Tell her... I kept the light. Tell her I was not... afraid. At the end." The lantern turns in his hands. "There is a shawl. Blue. She wove it, the winter I came here. It is in the chest... there." His chin lifts toward the corner of the lamp-house. "She is to have it back. Tell her it was warm. Every night. Tell her that."

He says nothing for a while. Then, as an afterthought: "She talks... too much. She will say I should have come home. Tell her... I had somewhere to be."

Answering your other question: the chest holds spare wicks and a flint, and the lamp is full. Oil is the real need, and Nessa and Berra have promised it. Your candles would only be a spare for a bad night, and ten would be a kindness. They are yours to leave or keep.

It is a little past noon. Greywater is a day's walk. If you leave now at a steady pace you will arrive after dark, around nine, and the valley road is not one you know. What does Brannoc do?

I fetch the blue shawl from the chest, fold it carefully into my pack, and leave five of my ten candles on the step beside Hob. "Five for a bad night, and I'll keep five for the road. I'll tell Maud every word: that you kept the light, that you weren't afraid, that the shawl was warm, and that you had somewhere to be."

Then I say goodbye with a hand on his cold shoulder and set out down the valley road at a steady pace, shield on my arm, Protection from Evil and Good ready. DM: if I'll arrive after dark, is there an inn or farmstead along the way where I could stop for the night rather than walk into Greywater at nine?

transcript.text: notebook: updated Lamp Watch

You fold the blue shawl into your pack, a soft, faded wool, still holding a faint smell of lamp oil and smoke. The five candles stand in a row on the step, and Hob looks down at them and then up at you. He cannot smile, but something shifts in the dull eyes.

"...Go well, healer," he says. "The light will be here."

You put a hand on his cold shoulder, and then you walk down the track in the early afternoon, past the Fenner fields and the ring of burnt lamps around the silent slab. A few people lift a hand from the furrows as you pass. Tam runs alongside for half a field, calls "Come back!", and gets no promise from you, only a nod.

Your question: yes. About six hours' walk down the valley road, two hours short of Greywater, stands the Millstone Inn, an old mill turned to lodging by a stout widow named Hesper Cole. It has clean beds, a common room, and a stable. You'd reach it near sunset, around seven. You could sleep there and arrive at Greywater fresh the next morning, instead of walking into a strange village in the dark. A bed there costs a few silver, and you have 15 gp.

The road is a pale ribbon through brown stubble and the first red leaves. The sun is warm, and your prayers are with you. You have time, and a message to carry.

What does Brannoc do on the road?

I walk at a steady pace, shield slung on my arm, humming Edda's hymn and keeping an eye on the ditches and the tree line. I'll stop at the Millstone Inn for the night, and reach Greywater fresh in the morning with the shawl and Hob's words.

If I meet anyone on the road who is hurt, lost, or frightened, I'll stop and help them. DM: how much of Hob's message do I remember exactly, and what would I say to Maud first when I find her at her loom?

input.description: Stout, sharp-eyed widow who keeps the Millstone Inn. Blunt, fair, and quick with a ladle. Has a carter's boy ill with a cough in the back room as Brannoc arrives, Day 3 ~7 PM.

transcript.result: entry Hesper Cole (person) created; relationship [27] added to Hesper Cole

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Hesper Cole; added 1 relationship to Hesper Cole

You remember Hob's words exactly, because you turned them over all the way down the road. He said:

"Tell her I kept the light. Tell her I was not afraid, at the end. There is a shawl, blue. She wove it the winter I came here. She is to have it back. Tell her it was warm, every night." And last, a little wryly: "She talks too much. She will say I should have come home. Tell her I had somewhere to be."

As for what you say first to Maud, that is yours to decide, but the simple truth is probably kindest. You could say your name and that you come from Hob, and that the shawl is in your pack, before you tell her the harder thing.

The road goes by without trouble. The valley is a slow curve of stubble fields, hedgerows hung with red hips, and a river glinting on your left. You pass a goatherd who nods and a tinker's cart going the other way, and nobody who needs a healer. You hum the whole way, and a boy fishing the bank stops to listen.

At ten to seven, with the sun low and gold behind you, the Millstone Inn comes up out of the river mist: a big old mill of gray stone, its waterwheel still turning, lamps lit in every window, smoke rising from two chimneys. A wide yard, a stable, and a signboard with a millstone painted on it hang over the door.

You step into the common room and the warmth hits you. It is clean and full of the smell of bread and onions. A stout woman with her sleeves rolled to the elbow looks you up and down, mace, shield, and amulet, and says, "Healer? Gods be thanked. Hesper Cole. I've a carter's boy in the back room with a cough that's been going on three days, and he's going the wrong way. Will you look at him? Bed and supper are yours, either way."

What does Brannoc do?

"Of course, Hesper. Take me to him, and bring a lamp and a cup of warm water with a little honey if you have it."

I'll kneel by the boy, listen to his breathing and feel his forehead and throat, and ask how long the cough has run, whether he's bringing up anything, and whether anyone else in the inn is sick. If it's more than I can ease with Medicine and rest, I'll use Cure Wounds or Healing Word as it fits.

time: 30 minutes later: Day 3, 7:20:42 PM

Hesper leads you through the kitchen to a narrow back room with a pallet under the eaves. Her lamp falls across a boy of about nine, flushed and sweat-damp, his hair stuck flat to his forehead. His name is Piper, and he does not stir when you kneel. His cough is wet and deep, and between spells his breath whistles.

Medicine (8): you don't get a clear read. His forehead is hot, his throat is rough, and the cough is plainly wet, but you cannot tell whether this is a bad chill that has settled low or something worse. His chest sounds muddy under your ear, but the pulse and the heat don't settle it either way, and you are honestly unsure.

What you do learn from asking is this. Hesper says the cough started three days ago, that he brings up a thick yellow-gray phlegm in the morning, and that no one else in the inn is sick. His father, Garn the carter, left him here and went on to Greywater with a load of cloth, and is due back in two days. The boy has taken little but water and broth.

You warm honey-water at the kitchen fire, and lift Piper to sip it. He takes half the cup and dozes off against your arm. Steam from a kettle in the room loosens his breath a little. Nothing you can do tonight will cure it outright, and Cure Wounds mends wounds, not fevers, so you hold it back.

It's about twenty past seven. Supper is on the table, Hesper has a free bed for you, and the boy is not worse, though he is not better. You could sit up with him, check him through the night, ask more of Hesper, or try a different approach tomorrow.

What does Brannoc do?

I eat a quick supper, then bring a stool to Piper's bedside and keep the kettle steaming. "Hesper, would you prop his shoulders up with a rolled blanket and wake me if his breathing changes? I'll sit with him tonight, since I promised never to let anyone suffer alone."

I'll check his breathing and brow every hour or so, humming low. DM: does Piper have a fever I could cool with a damp cloth, and can I try Medicine again with more time, or does anything in the room, like the phlegm or his lips, give me a clearer read?
dice Brannoc's second Medicine check after hours at the bedside, with phlegm, lips and fever to read, DC 12: 1d20+5 = 1d20 [8] + 5 = 13

input.add_to_description: Day 3 night: Brannoc's second Medicine read (13) found a lung fever (settled in the chest, no wound, no magic), not a simple chill. Cooling cloths, propped upright, steam and honey water; by ~1 AM fever eased from its peak. Cure Wounds cannot treat it; Lesser Restoration (level 3 for Brannoc) would end a disease. Garn the carter due back in two days.

transcript.result: added to Piper's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Piper

You eat Hesper's onion-and-barley stew, standing, and are back at the boy's side before the bowl is cold. Hesper props his shoulders on a rolled blanket without a word. She has done this before, for her own, and she says as much with a look. Then she leaves you the lamp and the kettle and tells you to knock on the wall if you need her.

Yes, he has a fever. His brow is hot and dry, and a cloth wrung in cool water takes the edge off it for a quarter of an hour at a time. You change it as it warms.

Medicine (13), a second look with hours of watching behind it: this time it comes clear. His lips are faintly blue-gray at the edges whenever the cough hits, and his breath takes a catch at the top of each inhalation, a small hitch. The phlegm in the cup is thick and rust-colored, not the pale spit of a cold. You are fairly sure now. This is a fever settled in the lungs, a true chest sickness, not a chill and not a wound. It is a fight his body has to win, with help. It is also why Cure Wounds was never going to touch it, and why Lesser Restoration, which ends a disease, would. It is a 2nd-level spell, and you cannot cast it until level 3.

What you can do is keep him upright, keep him cool, give him steam and honey water in small sips, and watch the breath. You do all of it through the night, humming low. Around the middle of the night his breathing eases from a rasp to a rattle, and a little before one o'clock his brow cools under your hand and a thin sweat breaks across it. He sleeps properly for the first time. He is not out of danger, but the worst of the climb is behind him.

It is twenty past midnight on Day 4. You are tired but steady. In a few hours Greywater's weaver will be waiting, and you may sleep for a while before the road, or stay longer with Piper.

What does Brannoc do?

I lay a hand on Piper's damp brow and let out a long breath. "Sleep well, little one." I'll get a few hours of rest on the stool beside him, then wake at first light to check his breathing once more before the road.

In the morning I'll tell Hesper plainly what the sickness is: keep him upright, cool, and sipping honey water, and send for a healer if the blue returns to his lips. I'll also leave a note for Garn the carter that his boy is mending and that Brannoc of Hollow Reach sat with him. Then I'll set out for Greywater with the shawl and Hob's words.

input.add_to_description: Day 4 dawn: fever low, breath easier, sleeping. Brannoc left instructions with Hesper (upright, cool, honey water, send for a healer if his lips go blue) and a note for Garn the carter. Healing Word only restores hit points, so Brannoc did not spend it.

transcript.result: added to Piper's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Piper

Your answer first: Healing Word restores hit points and nothing else, so it can't ease a fever or a bad chest. The sickness is not a wound. You can cast it and give him a little more strength for the road, but it wouldn't touch what is wrong, and I won't pretend it would. Your slots are better kept. The sleep, steam, and honey water are doing the real work.

You settle on the stool with your back against the wall, your hand where you can feel his breath. You sleep, in snatches, for six hours or so. Hesper wakes you at first gray with a mug of hot tea. Piper is awake and watching you with big, clear eyes. His fever has dropped to a mild warmth, his breath comes slow and mostly quiet, and he asks, hoarse, whether you are the man who hummed. You say you are. He says it helped, and goes back to sleep.

You tell Hesper plainly what it is: a sickness settled in the chest. Keep him upright, keep him cool, keep honey water in him in small sips, and send for a healer if the blue ever comes back to his lips. You write a few lines in the margin of a page of your prayer book, tear it neatly out, and leave it under the lamp for Garn: your son is mending, and Brannoc of Hollow Reach sat with him. Hesper refuses your coin and presses a heel of bread and a hard cheese into your hands. "Bed and board's for them as earn it," she says. "You did."

By seven you are on the road with the shawl in your pack. The mist lies thick on the river, and the sun is pale behind it. The road goes through low hills and pastures grazed gray-green, past a ford and a ruined chapel with its roof fallen in. It is quiet, and your steps and your humming are the only sound.

At about nine, the road bends and Greywater comes into view below, a cluster of slate roofs along the river, with racks of dyed wool drying red and blue and ochre in rows along the bank, and a weir turning white across the water. A small chapel stands at the near end with its door shut. A girl hauling a basket of yarn looks up, sees you, and stops. At the lower end of the village, by the weir, there is a house with a blue door.

What does Brannoc do?

I nod to the girl and ask gently, "Good morning. Could you tell me where Maud Marrow the weaver lives? I've come with word of her brother."

Then I walk down to the house with the blue door, shield slung on my back so I look less like a soldier, and knock. When she opens, I'll say, "Maud Marrow? My name is Brannoc, and I come from Hob. May I come in? I have something of yours in my pack, and I'd like to tell you about him in my own words."

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~9:20 AM: Brannoc reached her blue-door loom-house in Greywater with the shawl and Hob's words. She is a lean, grey-braided woman in her sixties with dyed-blue fingertips, talkative, who guessed from his face before he spoke. Hob had left in spring; they quarrelled about his staying at the Lamp.

transcript.result: added to Maud Marrow's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Maud Marrow

The girl with the yarn basket points without a word at the blue door, then crosses herself, a gesture of the old kind, and goes back to her work more slowly than before. You slip your shield onto your back, as you said, and walk down past the dye racks. The air smells of wet wool, woad, and wood smoke. The weir runs loud beside you.

The blue door is faded, the paint worn pale at the latch. From inside comes the steady knock and slide of a loom, a rhythm that has gone on so long it has become a kind of silence. You knock, and the sound stops.

The door opens on a lean woman in her sixties with a long gray braid, a leather apron, and fingertips stained blue to the second joint. She has Hob's long jaw and Hob's pale, patient eyes, but hers are quick and sharp. She looks at your amulet, at the mud on your boots, and at the way you are standing, and the color leaves her face before you have said a word.

You say it as you planned. Your name, that you come from Hob, that you have something of hers in your pack, and that you would tell her about him in your own words.

"Come in," she says, very quietly. She holds the door and steps back. The room is warm and crowded with wool and half-finished cloth, a great loom by the window, a kettle on the hob, and a single chair pulled up beside the fire, empty, with a folded blanket over its arm. She does not sit. She stands with both hands pressed flat on the back of the other chair.

"He's dead," she says. It is not a question. "Isn't he. I knew in the spring, when he went up that track and wouldn't be told. I said, 'Hob, you'll die in that damned lamp-house and nobody'll know for a month.'" Her voice cracks on the last word and steadies. "Say it. Say it plain, and then give me what you've got in that pack."

She is waiting. You have the shawl, Hob's words, and the whole of what happened. How does Brannoc tell her?

I take off my pack, set it on the table, and meet her eyes. "Yes, Maud. Hob died some time before the harvest feast, in the lamp-house, and nobody found him. I won't dress it up. But he did not leave the light, and he was not alone at the end: he kept it burning, and he saved a village by it."

I take out the blue shawl and hold it out in both hands. "He asked me to give you this. He said you wove it the winter he went up there, and I'm to tell you it was warm every night. He said to tell you he kept the light, that he wasn't afraid at the end." I add gently, "And he said you'd tell him he should have come home. He asked me to say he had somewhere to be."

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~10:45 AM: Brannoc gave Maud the shawl and Hob's words. Maud wept, then said she will come to the Lamp herself within the week with wool and a loom-stool to sit with him; she asks to be told when the Reach's rota begins. All parts of the quest done.

transcript.result: added to Lamp Watch's description; Lamp Watch is now done

transcript.text: notebook: updated Lamp Watch
sheet: lost 1 × Blue shawl (Maud Marrow's, to return to her); XP +100: 400

Maud does not move while you speak. When you reach the part about the light, her mouth tightens, and at "somewhere to be" something goes out of her, all at once, like a thread cut. She takes the shawl from you with both hands. For a moment she only holds it, thumbs moving over the weave, over a place near the hem where the pattern wanders.

"I dropped a stitch there," she says. "He used to say he liked it. Said it was the only part of it that was honestly mine and not the pattern's." She laughs, wetly, once. Then she sits down in the empty chair by the fire, with the blue wool bundled against her chest, and weeps like a woman who has put off weeping for half a year.

You do not hurry her, and you do not speak. You sit on the stool by the hearth with your hands loose between your knees, and when the kettle starts to sing you rise and take it off. You find the cups, and you pour. It is not much. It is what Edda would have done. She takes the cup without looking at it, and her hand is steady.

Some time later, perhaps an hour, she asks the questions. Did it hurt? You tell her you don't believe so. Was he alone? Not at the end, you say, and she does not ask more than that. She asks about the village, and you tell her about the Reach and the barn, about Cal and the others, and the five candles on the step. She listens with her chin on the shawl.

At last she wipes her face with her sleeve and looks at you with Hob's steady eyes in a living face. "Then I'll go up to him," she says. "Not today. I've work due, and a body can't go anywhere in this state. Within the week. I'll bring wool and a loom-stool and sit with the old fool until he tells me to go home." She nods slowly. "You'll tell them at the Reach to expect a woman who talks too much."

She presses your hand between both of hers, stained fingers warm. She will not take coin, or let you go without a loaf and a jar of honey from her shelf. Your XP stands at 400, and the shawl is where it belongs.

It is a quarter to eleven on Day 4. You are fed, rested, and full of prayers, with fifteen gold pieces and no one waiting on you. Hollow Reach has its rota, Hob has his sister, and the road runs on in two directions. The chapel at Greywater has no priest, and a girl with a yarn basket looked at you with a particular hope.

What does Brannoc do?

I thank Maud, take the loaf and honey, and tell her, "I'll tell the Reach to expect a woman who talks too much, and Hob will be glad of it." Then I walk up to the little chapel at the near end of the village and look for the girl with the yarn basket, to ask her who tends it now and who in Greywater has been sick or hurt with no healer to turn to.

The Life domain focuses on the vibrant positive energy—one of the fundamental forces of the universe—that sustains all life. The gods of life promote vitality and health through healing the sick and wounded, caring for those in need, and driving away the forces of death and undeath. Almost any non-evil deity can claim influence over this domain, particularly agricultural deities (such as Chauntea, Arawai, and Demeter), sun gods (such as Lathander, Pelor, and Re-Horakhty), gods of healing or endurance (such as Ilmater, Mishakal, Apollo, and Diancecht), and gods of home and community (such as Hestia, Hathor, and Boldrei).

input.description: Girl of about twelve in Greywater, a dyer's daughter who hauls yarn baskets and sweeps the village's priestless chapel. Hopeful and direct. Tells Brannoc the chapel has had no priest since the old one died two winters ago; the sick are tended by the weavers as best they can.

transcript.result: entry Wren (person) created; relationship [31] added to Wren

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Wren; added 1 relationship to Wren

Level 3 needs 900 XP, and you have 400, so you need 500 more. At 3rd level you would gain two 2nd-level slots, and Lesser Restoration is a Life domain spell for 3rd level. That means it would be always prepared and wouldn't count against your limit. It ends one disease or one condition (blinded, deafened, paralyzed, or poisoned), so it would have broken Piper's lung fever outright, and it would end a ghoul's paralysis on you or an ally.

You thank Maud once more, and she gives your hand a last squeeze and shoos you out. The loaf and a jar of honey go into your pack, and you walk up the lane, past the racks of drying wool, to the chapel.

It is a small slate-roofed building with a bell-cote and no bell. The door is unlocked. Inside it is swept clean, with wildflowers in a jar on a plain stone altar, and nobody in sight. The girl from the lane is standing on the step behind you, the yarn basket on her hip. Her name is Wren, a dyer's daughter of twelve or so, and she looks at you directly.

"Old Father Tulle died two winters back," she says. "Nobody's come since. I sweep it, because somebody should." She hesitates. "People still come to sit. When they're frightened."

She tells you who is ill, when you ask, and she's thorough about it. Three people in Greywater are suffering with no one to see to them. A weaver named Osric has a scalded forearm that never closed and is going red at the edges. A woman named Ilsa Dunmore has been coughing for a fortnight, and her baby has the same rattle. And old Perrin Gale, who dyes in the sheds, fell from a rack and hasn't walked straight since, and he won't let anyone look at it.

You have all three prayers ready, three 1st-level slots, and Channel Divinity. It is a little past eleven in the morning. You could see all three, or only one first.

What does Brannoc do?

"Thank you, Wren. Will you take me to Osric first? A scald going red at the edges won't wait, and I'll see Ilsa and her baby next, then Perrin, who I'll ask kindly rather than force."

I'll start with Medicine to clean and look at the burn, and use Cure Wounds only if it needs more than clean linen and honey. I'll keep a slot for Perrin's fall and ask Wren to come along and tell him I'm a friend of Maud Marrow's.
