input.description: Middle-aged weaver of Greywater with a scalded forearm from a dye vat three weeks ago that went red and angry. Brannoc cleaned it, drew the matter with a honey dressing and linen, and judged it will heal without magic if kept clean and changed daily. Taught Wren to change the dressing.

transcript.result: entry Osric (person) created; relationship [32] added to Osric

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Osric; added 1 relationship to Osric

Wren leads you along the river to a long dye-shed where Osric sits on an overturned tub with his arm wrapped in a filthy rag. He is a thick-armed man, gray at the temples, and he eyes you warily until Wren says you are a friend of Maud Marrow's. After that, he lets you unwind the cloth.

Medicine (17): the forearm tells you everything. It is a deep scald, three weeks old, split in two places along the inner arm, and angry red at the margins, with a little yellow weeping. It smells faintly sour. The flesh is hot but not black, there are no red streaks running toward the elbow, and he has no fever. It is festering, not rotting. You are confident it will mend without magic if it is kept clean.

You do what it needs. You wash it with warm salt water, trim the dead skin back to the clean edge with the small knife from your pack, and spread honey thin over the raw places, honey from Maud's own jar. Then you wrap it in clean linen, firmly but not tight. Osric swears through his teeth and does not pull away. You show Wren how to change the dressing each morning and each night, with boiled water and fresh honey, and she nods gravely and repeats every step back to you.

"It'll close in a fortnight," you tell him. "Keep it out of the vats. If the red climbs above the wrist, or you take a fever, send for me." He nods, a little humbled. "Thank you," he says gruffly. "I'd about decided to lose the arm."

You saved your slot. It is a quarter to noon. Wren takes you next to a low house on the village's east lane, where a thin, tired woman stands in the doorway with a baby on her shoulder. You hear the rattle in the baby's chest from three paces away. This is Ilsa Dunmore.

What does Brannoc do?

I smile at Ilsa and keep my voice soft. "Goodwife, I'm Brannoc, a friend of Maud Marrow's. May I come in and listen to the little one's chest, and to yours? I'll ask how long you've both been coughing, and whether the baby is feeding."

Inside I'll sit her by the fire and check the baby's lips for blue, the fever, and the breathing, then use Medicine with honey-water, steam and propped sleeping, as with Piper. DM: Ilsa's husband, if there is one, and how old is the baby?
dice Brannoc's Medicine check on Ilsa and her baby's cough, DC 12: 1d20+5 = 1d20 [11] + 5 = 16

input.description: Thin, tired young mother in Greywater with a two-week cough; her baby daughter Tessa (about four months) has the same rattle. Husband Garrick Dunmore is a boatman away upriver hauling dyestuffs, due back in about four days.

transcript.result: entry Ilsa Dunmore (person) created; relationship [33] added to Ilsa Dunmore

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Ilsa Dunmore; added 1 relationship to Ilsa Dunmore
time: 50 minutes later: Day 4, 12:35:42 PM

Ilsa lets you in with a tired, grateful nod. She is perhaps twenty-three, hollow under the eyes, and when she says her husband's name it is with the care of someone not letting herself miss him too much. Garrick Dunmore is a boatman, upriver hauling dyestuffs, due back in about four days. The baby is Tessa, a girl of four months, round-faced and flushed, with a damp little fist knotted in her mother's collar.

You sit Ilsa by the fire, and you ask, and you listen.

Medicine (16): the picture comes clear enough. Ilsa's cough is dry and deep, of a fortnight's standing, with an ache under the ribs and a night sweat. It is a lingering chest cold that never quite cleared, made worse by tiredness and a smoky, closed room. It's not the lung fever Piper had. The baby's breath is rapid but not labored, and the rattle is wet and loose, not tight. Her lips are pink, she is feeding, and she has no fever above warmth. Tessa has caught her mother's cough, and is likely to mend as her mother mends.

What would help most is plain. You have Ilsa lie back with her shoulders propped, and you give her warm honey-water in sips, and you show her how to keep the baby upright against her chest when she sleeps. You open the shutter a hand's breadth to let the smoke out. You show her how to steam a kettle by the bed. You leave a third of Maud's honey, and you tell her to eat when she can and to send Wren for you at once if Tessa's lips go blue, if she won't feed, or if she turns hot and still. It is not magic. It is the kind of care that was missing, and she cries a little with the relief of having someone say plainly that her baby is not dying.

You spend nothing from your slots. It is twenty-five to one. Perrin Gale is waiting in the dye-sheds, the one who won't let anyone look at his fall, and Wren stands in the lane with her basket, watching you.

What does Brannoc do?

"Thank you, Wren. Take me to Perrin, and tell him on the way that I'm a friend of Maud's and I only want to look, not to fuss."

At the dye-sheds I'll keep my distance, sit on an upturned tub where he can see my hands, and talk about the work first, how long he's dyed and what colors, before asking how he fell and what hurts. I'll offer to look at his back or leg only if he agrees, and I'll keep Cure Wounds ready in case it's a true injury.

input.description: Old dyer of Greywater, proud and gruff, who fell from a drying rack a month ago and has walked crooked since; won't let anyone look at it. Brannoc won his trust by asking about the dye work. Injury: left hip and lower back; Brannoc's first read inconclusive (Medicine 8). DM ruling: Cure Wounds restores hit points only and cannot unset an old crooked injury.

transcript.result: entry Perrin Gale (person) created; relationship [34] added to Perrin Gale

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Perrin Gale; added 1 relationship to Perrin Gale

Wren walks ahead of you on the way down and tells Perrin from the shed door that you are a friend of Maud Marrow's and want only to look. The old man grumbles from the dark inside that he has seen enough healers to last a hundred years, and none of them ever came to a clean thing.

You do as you planned. You sit on an upturned tub where he can see your hands, rest the mace and shield against the wall, and say nothing about his fall. You ask about his dyes instead: how long he has been at it, what the madder does that the woad cannot, where he gets his weld. He is a long time answering, and then he cannot stop. He has been dyeing for fifty-one years, and he knows the river's moods like a woman's. Persuasion (17): by the time his hands have stopped tightening on the tub's edge, he is the one who says it, gruffly, to the vat. "Fell from the rack. Third rung. A month back."

He lets you look, once you ask, and only as far as he will.

Medicine (8): you can't make a clear read of it. He winces when you press his left hip and lower back, and the hip sits a little higher than the right, as if the whole frame has set at a slant. You can't tell whether it's a deep bruise that has knotted the muscle, a hip knocked out of its seat and left, or a cracked bone that healed crooked. He walks on it, and he won't go to bed. Each would need something different.

One thing you can say. Cure Wounds restores hit points, and by my ruling it does not unset a month-old hurt that has already healed wrong. It could ease the wearing damage, but it would not make a crooked hip straight. You have all three slots, though, and you could spend one if you want to try anyway.

It's about twenty past one. Perrin is watching you with wary, tired eyes. Wren is perched on a drying rack, quiet for once.

What does Brannoc do?

"Master Perrin, I can't promise to straighten what's healed crooked, but I can try to ease the ache and the wear on that hip. May I lay a hand on it and say a short prayer? It won't hurt, and it costs you nothing."

If he agrees, I'll cast Cure Wounds on him at 1st level and see what it does. Either way, I'll show him a gentle stretch, and ask him to keep a stool at his vat so he isn't standing all day. DM: is there a bonesetter or surgeon in Greywater or nearby I could send him to for the hip itself?
dice Cure Wounds on Perrin Gale (1d8 + WIS 3 + Disciple of Life 3): 1d8+6 = 1d8 [4] + 6 = 10
sheet: Brannoc casts Cure Wounds at level 1; level-1 spell slots: 2/3

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~1:50 PM: agreed to a prayer; Cure Wounds eased the ache. Hip still sits crooked. Brannoc showed him a stretch and told him to keep a stool at the vat; recommended Mother Aldith of Stonebridge.

transcript.result: added to Perrin Gale's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Perrin Gale

He is silent for a moment. Then he gives a short, grudging nod, the nod of a man agreeing to a thing he plainly thinks is foolish. "Say your prayer, then. Mind the hip."

You kneel and lay a hand on the small of his back, over the knotted muscle, and say it low. The warmth gathers and goes in. It is not a great working, and you can feel it spread through the band of tightness and then stop at the place where the bone sits wrong, like water finding a wall. Ten points of life go into him. Perrin draws a long breath through his nose, shoulders dropping an inch, and lets it out slowly.

"Well," he says. "That's the first night I'd sleep through in a month."

The hip itself is unchanged. When he stands, it still sits a little high, and he still carries it with the same cautious lean. But the grinding wince has gone out of his face. You show him a gentle stretch, one knee drawn slowly to the chest while lying flat on his back on a blanket, and you ask him to keep a stool at the vat and sit between pours, however much he scorns it. He grumbles that stools are for women and bairns. Wren says something sharp from the rack, and he scowls and takes the stool.

Yes, there is a bonesetter. Mother Aldith keeps a house in Stonebridge, the market town a day's walk further down the valley past Greywater. She sets hips and the like, and is known for breaking and resetting bones that healed wrong, which is hard, but it is the only thing that will straighten his. Perrin says he will think on it, which, from a man like him, you take to mean maybe.

You have two 1st-level slots left. It is ten to two in the afternoon, and the village has been seen to. Wren is looking at you and the chapel and the road with a question in her face. Your prayers will come back by morning if you rest here, and Hollow Reach and the Lamp are a day behind you, with the road down to Stonebridge ahead.

What does Brannoc do?

I turn to Wren and kneel to her level. "You've done more than any one person should for Greywater, Wren. Let's sit in the chapel a moment, and I'll show you the dressing for Osric again and how to tell a fever from a chill, so there's someone here who knows."

I'll stay the night in Greywater, sweeping the chapel with her and keeping watch over Ilsa's baby, then rest to restore my prayers before heading down to Stonebridge. DM: does Mother Aldith have a reputation I should know of, and could I ask her to take on Wren as an apprentice?

input.add_to_description: Reputation (told to Brannoc Day 4 by Maud Marrow and Perrin Gale): blunt, loud, no patience for fools, and the best bonesetter in the valley; has had three apprentices, two of whom stayed. Wants coin, not charity, from those who can pay, but never turns away the poor. Owes Maud a favour (Maud wove her winter blankets).

transcript.result: added to Mother Aldith's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

In the chapel, Wren sits cross-legged on the cold flags with her yarn basket still beside her. She drinks it all in as if she were hungry for it. You show her Osric's dressing again, slowly, with your hands over hers: boiled water, honey thin, linen firm but not tight. You teach her the plain signs. A fever is hot, dry, and still. A chill shivers and sweats and comes and goes. A baby's breath is counted against a slow count of sixty, and blue at the lips is the thing you never wait on. She repeats each step back, and where she gets one wrong she says it again until it is right. You also teach her the first line of Edda's hymn, and she hums it badly and with great seriousness.

Your questions: Maud and Perrin both had something to say about Mother Aldith by the time you came for supper. She is blunt, loud, and short of patience for fools, and she is the best bonesetter in the valley. She has had three apprentices and two of them stayed. She wants coin from those who can pay, but never turns the poor from her door. Maud weaves her winter blankets, so she owes her a favour. Whether she'd take Wren is another matter, and one the dyer's daughter's parents must also answer. You write a short letter of recommendation in the margin of your prayer book and tear the leaf out. Wren holds it as if it were made of glass.

The evening goes on. You sweep the chapel with her, you set the kettle on for Ilsa, and you go twice to the low house on the east lane to count the baby's breaths against a slow sixty. Tessa sleeps easy on her mother's shoulder both times, the rattle looser than before.

It is nearly nine at night, and you have settled onto a pallet in the little chapel. Your prayers will return at dawn when you finish the long rest. You can change your prepared list then.

How does Brannoc spend the last of the evening, and which prayers does he prepare?

I spend the last of the evening kneeling at the plain stone altar, thanking the gods for Piper's mending, Osric's arm, and little Tessa's easy sleep, and humming Edda's hymn until Wren drowses off on the bench with her yarn basket in her lap. Then I lay out my pallet and let the long rest take me.

For tomorrow I'll keep my list as it is: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready. I'll go down to Stonebridge in the morning to find Mother Aldith for Perrin and Wren, and keep my eyes open for the next place with no healer.

input.add_to_description: Day 5 dawn: Brannoc slept in the chapel; Osric, Ilsa, Tessa and Perrin tended; Wren taught basic nursing and given a letter for Mother Aldith. Greywater now knows a healer was kind to them. Brannoc heads to Stonebridge.

transcript.result: added to Greywater's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Greywater

You kneel at the altar a long while, and the words come without being sought, thanks for a boy who mends, for an arm that will keep its use, for a baby asleep against her mother. You hum until Wren's chin sinks to her chest and the yarn basket slides in her lap. You carry the basket to the bench beside her and lay your blanket over her shoulders. Then you lay out your pallet, the amulet in your fist, and the old stone chapel holds the night around you like a hand.

You wake at ten to five, before the first gray, rested and clear. Hit points 17 of 17, all three slots and your Channel Divinity restored, and both Hit Dice back. Your list is as you set it: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready.

The chapel is cold and dim, with the first thin light at the window. Wren has curled up on the bench with your blanket, still asleep. Someone has left a small wooden bowl of porridge by the altar, still faintly warm, with a spoon across it and a twist of blue wool tied to the handle, Maud's mark. By the door, Osric, awake before dawn as weavers are, leans on the frame with his bandaged arm held against his chest, and gives you a nod that says more than he'd say aloud.

In the lane outside, the river is loud over the weir, and a single lamp is lit in Ilsa's window. Stonebridge is a day's walk down the valley. You carry the letter for Mother Aldith and Perrin's hip, and Wren's question, which is still unanswered. You can leave now, in the dark, or wait for the sun and Wren's waking.

What does Brannoc do?

I eat Maud's porridge standing by the altar, then wait for Wren to wake rather than slip away from her. When she stirs, I'll tell her I'm leaving for Stonebridge with her letter for Mother Aldith, and that her parents should hear it from her first before any road is chosen.

Before I go, I'll check Ilsa's baby once more by counting her breaths, and thank Osric for the nod. DM: is Wren's father or mother awake yet, and would they let me speak with them about the apprenticeship before I leave?

input.add_to_description: Day 5: surname Reed. Her parents Corwin and Hale agreed to a one-month trial with Mother Aldith, with Maud Marrow to travel with her.

transcript.result: added to Wren's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Wren

You eat Maud's porridge standing, warm all the way down, and wash the bowl at the chapel's well. You wait. It is not long. Wren stirs at the first full light, blinks at your blanket, and sits up in alarm as if she had overslept her own life. You tell her you are going to Stonebridge with her letter, and that her parents should hear it from her first, before any road is chosen. She goes very still, and then she nods hard and straightens her braid with both hands.

Before you go you count Tessa's breaths again, a slow sixty by the window. They are easy and even, her fist loose in her mother's hair. Ilsa, drowsy, mouths a thank you. You thank Osric, too, and his mouth twitches into something nearly a smile.

Her parents are already awake, as dyers are, and are already at the vats. The father, Corwin, is a large, quiet man with arms stained to the shoulder, and the mother, Hale, is quick and careful and does not stop working while she listens. You tell them plainly: that Wren has a mind for tending and a steady hand, that you have written to a bonesetter in Stonebridge on her behalf, that it is only a letter and a visit, and that the choice is theirs and hers.

Persuasion (19): they listen all through, and Hale is the one who asks the hard questions: how long, who feeds her, who keeps her safe, what happens if it is not a good fit. You answer honestly each time, including that you cannot promise it will suit. Corwin wipes his hands and says to the vat, not to you, "She's been sweeping that chapel since she was eight. Nobody asked her." At last they agree, on conditions: a one-month trial only, with Maud Marrow to go with her to Stonebridge when the weather holds, and a return at harvest if either of them wishes it. Wren holds her letter against her chest, and she does not cry, but she does not trust her voice.

It is twenty past six on Day 5. The village is waking, with smoke rising and the weir loud. You have all three prayers, a letter delivered, a hip to speak for, and the valley road down to Stonebridge, a day's walk, which you could take now.

What does Brannoc do?

I thank Corwin and Hale with a hand over my heart, then crouch to Wren. "A month's trial, and you can always come home. Keep up the dressings and the counting of breaths until Maud takes you down, and keep sweeping that chapel."

Then I shoulder my pack and set out down the valley road toward Stonebridge, to find Mother Aldith, speak for Perrin's hip, and see who else along the way has no healer. DM: how far is Stonebridge by the road, and does it have a temple of my faith where Shelter of the Faithful would give me and my companions free care?

input.description: Grey, cheerful priest who keeps the house of the healing faith at Stonebridge, a hospice of twelve beds beside a plain shrine. Brannoc has a claim on shelter and care there under Shelter of the Faithful. Overworked, short of hands, and eager for another healer.

transcript.result: entry Brother Ansel (person) created; relationship [40] added to Brother Ansel

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Brother Ansel; added 1 relationship to Brother Ansel

Wren stands straighter when you crouch to her. She says "Yes, sir," and then, after a moment, "Brannoc," and you both smile at it. She promises the dressings, the breath-counting, and the chapel, and she says it as one makes a vow. Corwin gives you a rough, sincere handclasp. Hale presses a twist of dried apple slices into your hand without looking up from the vat.

Your questions: Stonebridge is a day's walk by the valley road, about eight hours at a steady pace, and you will arrive in the afternoon. And yes, there is a house of your faith. It is a small hospice of twelve beds with a plain shrine, kept by a Brother Ansel, and under Shelter of the Faithful you and any companions can expect free healing and care there, provided you bring any material components yourself.

The road goes without trouble. The valley widens as you go, with the river broad and slow on your left. The fields are better kept, the fences are whole, and you pass a mill, a toll-hut with a bored keeper, and an ox-cart whose driver gives you a lift for two miles in exchange for a song, which you give him badly. You count the miles by the shadows.

At twenty past two the town rises out of the valley haze: Stonebridge, a walled huddle of timber and tile at the foot of a long stone bridge of seven arches. Carts queue at the gate, and drovers shout, and a bell somewhere rings the hour. Beyond the wall, over the roofs, you can see a bell-cote, a market cross, and a thin line of smoke from what must be a forge.

At the gate a guardsman in a patched tabard looks you over, the mace, the shield, the amulet, and waves you through with a tired "Healer? Hospice is past the tannery on the left. They'll be glad of you. We had a cart go over on the bridge this morning, three hurt, and Ansel's only got the two hands."

It is a little past two. You have your prayers, and the hospice is a short walk from the gate. Mother Aldith's house is somewhere in the town, and Perrin's hip is a promise you carry. What does Brannoc do?

"Then the hospice first. Three hurt from a cart can't wait on my errands."

I hurry past the tannery with my shield on my arm, find Brother Ansel, and say, "I'm Brannoc, a cleric of the Life domain, and I have three healing prayers ready. Tell me who is worst off and where to start." I'll triage by Medicine, put my Cure Wounds and Healing Word where they'll save the most, and ask about Mother Aldith once the wounded are settled.

You are through the gate and past the tannery in three minutes, and the hospice is easy to find: a low, long building of whitewashed timber, a plain shrine with a lamp burning at the end of it, and a green door standing open. Inside, Brother Ansel, a lean, gray, bright-eyed man in his sixties with a bandage roll in one hand and a bowl of water in the other, looks up and sees the amulet. "Edda's," he says. "I knew her, a long time ago. Gods bless her. Come, come."

You give your name and what you carry, three healing prayers, and he points with the bowl. Three cots, one apprentice, and no healer in the house but him.

Medicine (20, a natural 20): you move through the three of them with an ease that surprises you, and the whole picture comes clear in a minute.

Rudd Fenwick, the carter, has a shattered thigh and a steady, deep bleed through the dressing, and he is the worst off. Without help, he will not be alive by dark. Imma, an eleven-year-old girl who was riding with him, has a head knock, vomits, is drowsy and slow to answer, and should be watched through the night but is not in immediate danger. Tobin, a boy of nine, has a badly crushed ankle that will need Mother Aldith's setting, and he is shivering with shock.

And you notice what nobody else has. Round Tobin's ankle, under the swelling, are long gray finger-marks, four of them, spread wide, with a cold, blue-white burn at each tip like frost-bite. They smell faintly of the same sour grave-air as the hole at the Long Cut. The carter, half out of his head, keeps muttering that something pulled the wheel under the second arch. The horse bolted before the cart went over. The apprentice thinks he is raving.

You have three 1st-level slots, Cure Wounds and Healing Word both ready, and Channel Divinity's Preserve Life, with 10 hit points to divide among those at half their maximum or less. How do you spend them, and who do you ask about the bridge?

I go to Rudd first and cast Cure Wounds on him at 1st level, hand pressed over the dressing, to stop the bleed. Then I spend Preserve Life on Imma and Tobin, giving Imma 4 and Tobin 6 since the knock and the shock are what threaten them tonight, and I keep my last two slots in reserve for whatever the bridge has in store.

"Brother Ansel, those gray marks on Tobin's ankle are the same I saw in Hollow Reach. Ghouls. Who was on the bridge when it happened, and does anyone go under the second arch after dark? Please keep a lamp lit by every cot tonight."

Boatmen avoid it after dark; the bridge-watchman Hodd Pell says lamp-oil goes missing from the arch niches and he hears 'something scratching on the damp stone' at night. Gray handprints found on Tobin's ankle came from below the second arch.
relationships: may connect to the barrow-crypt of the [[Long Cut]]

Rudd first. You press your palm over the sodden dressing and the prayer takes, eight points of life going in, and under your hand the bleed slows, then stops. His gray face darkens to something living, and he draws a long, shuddering breath. The shattered thigh is still broken, but he will not die tonight.

Then Preserve Life, with the holy symbol held up and the light going out from it in a low gold wash over the two children's cots. Here the rules ask something of you. The channel can restore a creature only to half its hit point maximum and no further, and these children are small and badly hurt. Imma has little to give back, since her knock has taken her nearly to nothing, and so does Tobin. Between them, the prayer can restore only 3 points each, and the rest of its ten points find no place to go. It is less than you asked for, and it is what the rule allows. Imma's eyes clear and her vomiting stops. Tobin's shivering eases, and the blue goes from his lips. Neither is out of danger, but both are held.

Your Channel Divinity is spent until your next rest, and you have two 1st-level slots left.

Ansel answers your question over a basin, wringing a cloth. "Hodd Pell was the bridge-watchman this morning, and a dozen carters. I'll send the boy for him." He lowers his voice. "The second arch. There's an old river-stair under it, the Drowned Stair, down to a cellar-vault older than the bridge. Boatmen won't go under it after dark. Hodd says the lamp-oil goes missing from the arch niches, and he's heard something scratching on the wet stone. I thought it was rats." He looks at Tobin's ankle. "Gods keep us, I think I was wrong."

He does as you ask. By half past three there is a lamp lit by every cot, and a bowl of oil beside each, and his apprentice, a freckled boy named Pip, runs to fetch Hodd.

It is a quarter past three. The bridge is a short walk, the light is good, and the dark is about three hours off. You have two prayers left and no Channel Divinity, and a vault under the second arch that you have never seen.

What does Brannoc do?

I wait for Hodd Pell to arrive and sit with him by Rudd's cot. "Hodd, I'm Brannoc. Tell me everything you saw this morning, and how long the oil has been going missing from the niches. Have any boatmen or children gone near the Drowned Stair, and is the stair door locked or barred?"

Then I'll go look at the second arch in daylight, with Hodd and one or two of the town guard, and I'll do nothing hasty. I want to see the stair, the missing lamps and the marks, and then decide whether to seal it with iron and stone and light, as we did at the Long Cut.

Hodd Pell is a lean, stooped man in his fifties with a lantern-keeper's callused hands, and he sits by Rudd's cot turning his hat round and round. He tells it plainly. This morning he saw the cart come onto the bridge, a good bay horse, a steady driver. At the second arch the horse screamed and bolted, and the cart's near wheel dropped into the gap by the parapet as if the stone had grabbed it. Then the cart went over. He saw nothing in the water but a thick cold mist that lingered a minute under the arch.

The oil has been going from the niches for a month, he says. A flask a night, sometimes two, from the second and third arches only. He blamed boatmen. No children go near it, because the stair is gated, an old iron-banded grating at the foot of the bridge steps, its padlock rusted half through. He has not been down in thirty years.

You answer your own questions where you can. The town has a watch captain, Captain Maren Voss, a scarred, sharp-eyed woman of forty with a limp, who is sceptical but fair. Ansel is the only priest of your faith in the town. And on the cost, one flask of oil is a silver piece, so with 15 gp you could buy as many as a hundred and fifty, far more than you could carry, and fifty would last any reasonable expedition.

Voss listens to your account in the guardhouse doorway with her arms folded, and then gives you two guards, Bede, a big slow man with a halberd, and Corra, a young woman with a short sword and a quick eye. By a quarter past four you are on the bridge with Hodd and the guards, looking over the parapet at the second arch.

Perception (14): the stair door is as Hodd said, a rusted grating, but a rusted chain hangs loose and the padlock is not rusted through; it has been forced from inside. The lowest steps are wet. The niches on the arch hold two empty lamp-flasks and one overturned, and beside the third niche, on the stone, are long gray finger-marks, four of them, spread wide, like the ones on Tobin's ankle.

From below there is a faint, slow scrape on stone. It stops when Corra shifts her boots.

The sun is still high, and the dark is about two hours off. You have two prayers left and no Channel Divinity. What does Brannoc do?

I raise a hand to the guards to keep still and speak low. "Not a sound, and nobody goes down yet. Daylight is our friend, so Bede, buy fifty flasks of oil and bring two more guards and a sledge and iron bar, while Corra and I watch the grating."

Then I ask Hodd quietly, "Does the vault have any other way out, like a drain or a landing on the river bank, and is there a stone or iron slab we could seal the stair with?" I'll cast Protection from Evil and Good on myself only if the scraping comes up the steps, and keep Shield of Faith ready.

You keep the guards still and your voice low. Bede goes off at a trot. Corra stays beside you at the parapet with her hand on her sword, and neither of you says a word. Below, the scraping comes twice more, slow and patient, and stops each time you shift your feet.

Hodd answers in a whisper. The water at the stair's foot is about knee-deep this time of year, since the river is low in autumn. It runs waist-deep in spring floods. The vault has a grated drain culvert opening to the river, too small for a man, and an old tale of a sealed passage called the Dead Road, running toward the burial hill outside the walls. He has never seen it. For sealing, there are spare bridge capstones stacked in the quay yard, and the grating itself is iron-banded oak, good for wedging.

You could hang lamps from above, and you do. Hodd fetches two long lamp-poles from the bridge, and you hang four lit lanterns over the parapet, so that gold light falls down the stair's throat and shines on the wet steps. The scraping does not come again for a long while. You take that as a good sign, though you do not trust it.

Bede returns at half past five, red-faced and sweating, with two more guards, a sledge, an iron bar, and fifty flasks of oil in two sacks. That cost 5 gp, so you have 10 left. The sun is lower now, the river is going copper, and the first long shadows lie across the quay. Dusk is about an hour off.

You have two 1st-level slots, no Channel Divinity, Protection from Evil and Good ready with its powder, and Shield of Faith. Five guards and Hodd stand ready, the capstones are in the yard, and below the arch the lamplight holds.

What does Brannoc do?

"Good work, Bede. Here's the plan: we seal the stair, not fight in the dark. Two guards and Hodd bring a capstone from the quay yard to the grating, and we wedge the iron bar and the old oak through the bars, then pack the gap with stone and mortar-clay before dusk."

"Before we set it, I'll pour oil down the steps and light it, so the stair burns bright while we work. Corra and Bede hold the grating with halberds and keep the lanterns burning, and if anything climbs, we step back and let the fire and the lamps hold it. I'll stand at the front with my shield, and cast Shield of Faith on myself the moment I hear claws on the steps."

DM: do I know whether any of these guards has fought ghouls or the paralysis before, and should I warn them to stay out of reach of the claws?

Your answer to the guards first: neither Bede nor Corra has fought a ghoul. Corra knows only the tavern tales, and Bede has never seen one. They don't know about the paralysing claws, which you do. So you gave the warning in a harsh whisper while hauling the first capstone to the grating, to stay out of reach of those claws. It was not enough time to drill it into them.

Then you poured the oil down the steps and lit it, as you planned. A sheet of low yellow fire ran down the old stairs and licked at the wet stone, while the four lanterns above shone gold. The crew worked. The first capstone slid against the grating, the oak wedges went through the bars, Hodd tamped clay into the gaps, and Athletics (20) said the work went fast and sure. You were nearly done.

Then the stair roared. A ghoul came up through the burning, gray skin blackening and sizzling where the fire caught it, with a second shape lurching in the smoke behind. It slammed against the half-sealed grating, and one long arm snaked through the bars and raked your chest, a perfect, ugly blow. The claws bit deep through your chain mail, and your body locked stiff, paralysed for one long moment, while Bede and Corra stabbed at the thing through the bars. You came free at the end of that same heartbeat, which is the only reason you are standing.

Now it is your turn, round 2. You are at 7 of 17 HP. The ghoul at the grating is bloodied, with fire on its skin and two spear wounds. It clawed at you again and missed. Bede and Corra hold either side of you, 11 HP each, and a second ghoul waits behind the first. The grating is mostly sealed, but not quite. You still have two 1st-level slots, your mace, and no Channel Divinity.

What does Brannoc do?

I step back out of the claws' reach and cast Shield of Faith on myself as a bonus action, then use my action to cast Healing Word on myself. "Bede, Corra, keep spearing from the sides and stay clear of that arm!"

If I can, I'll back up another pace so the ghoul has to reach through the half-sealed grating at an angle, and finish the capstone with the guards once it's bloodied enough to flinch away from the fire.

RULE Casting Time:
Most spells require a single action to cast, but some spells require a bonus action, a reaction, or much more time to cast.

#### Bonus Action

A spell cast with a bonus action is especially swift. You must use a bonus action on your turn to cast the spell, provided that you haven't already taken a bonus action this turn. You can't cast another spell during the same turn, except for a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action.

#### Reactions

Some spells can be cast as reactions. These spells take a fraction of a second to bring about and are cast in response to some event. If a spell can be cast as a reaction, the spell description tells you exactly when you can do so.

#### Longer Casting Times

Certain spells (including spells cast as rituals) require more time to cast: minutes or even hours. When you cast a spell with a casting time longer than a single action or reaction, you must spend your action each turn casting the spell, and you must maintain your concentration while you do so (see "Concentration" below). If your concentration is broken, the spell fails, but you don't expend a spell slot. If you want to try casting the spell again, you must start over.

input.add_to_description: Day 5 dusk: two ghouls (A and B) came up the stair and were killed at the grating by Brannoc and the guards Bede and Corra. The grating was then sealed with a capstone, oak wedges and clay. Any further ghouls and the Dead Road passage remain unknown.

transcript.result: added to The Drowned Stair's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Drowned Stair

Sacred Flame drops out of the sky onto the crouching ghoul. It fails to dodge and the radiance burns through what the fire and the bolt left of it. It falls back from the bars and doesn't rise again. The scraping on the steps stops, and the only sound is the oil hissing on the wet stone.

Nobody cheers. Corra lets out a long breath, and Bede sits down hard against the parapet with his halberd across his knees. Then the work starts again. All five guards and Hodd put their shoulders to the capstone and drive it home against the bars. The oak wedges go in, the clay is packed hard, and the iron bar is jammed across. When it's done the grating is stopped solid, with no gap anywhere. You hold your lantern to the seam and see no crack to put a finger in, unlike the Long Cut. Hodd mutters that he'll add a second stone in the morning and have the watch look at the niches every night.

For the two ghouls at the grating, you have 800 XP, 100 short of level 3. Bede has 5 HP, a bruised pride and no lasting harm. Corra is unhurt. Your spell slots are all gone, and Channel Divinity with them. The gray finger-marks on the stone are the only sign of what came up.

It's about eleven minutes past six, with the light failing and the river going dark. Down the stair there may be more of them, and the old tale of the Dead Road is still only a tale. Ansel's cots are a short walk away, with Rudd, Imma and Tobin in them, and Mother Aldith still has to be found.

What does Brannoc do?

I check Bede first, kneeling to look him over and bind what needs binding, then tell Hodd, "Keep two guards on this grating tonight with every lantern lit, and send for me at once if the scratching starts again."

Then I head back to Brother Ansel's hospice to look in on Rudd, Imma and Tobin, take the free bed and the long rest that Shelter of the Faithful promises, and in the morning ask Ansel where I can find Mother Aldith. DM: how far is Bede from needing real care, and is Mother Aldith's house near the hospice?

input.add_to_description: Day 5 evening: Brannoc has not yet met her. Her house in Stonebridge is a few streets from the hospice (Ansel can direct him).

transcript.result: added to Mother Aldith's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

You kneel by Bede at the parapet and look him over by lantern-light. There's no wound on him, only the stiffness of the paralysis wearing off and a bruise on his hip from the stones. His grip is firm and his eyes are clear. You turn his hand over, count his pulse, make him follow your finger, and wrap the hip in a strip of linen. He grins weakly and says he's never been so glad of a spear. For answer to your question: he's nowhere near needing real care. A night's rest and a hot meal will mend him. If his breath goes short, or numbness lingers in his limbs past morning, send him to Ansel. Corra is untouched.

You tell Hodd what you said you would. Two guards on the grating all night, every lantern lit, and a runner to the hospice at the first scratch. Hodd nods and says he'll stand the first watch himself, since he's the one who didn't look for thirty years.

Mother Aldith's house is on the tanners' lane, about four streets from the hospice, a short walk. Ansel can point you to it in the morning.

At the hospice, the lamps burn by every cot as you asked. Rudd sleeps with his splinted thigh propped high, and his colour is better. Imma wakes enough to tell you her head hurts "less than a drum", and Tobin sleeps curled round his bad ankle with his fist against his mouth. Ansel presses a bowl of lentil broth into your hands and shows you a cot at the end of the row, under the shrine lamp. Shelter of the Faithful, as promised, and no coin asked.

You sleep from ten to nine at night. Your prayers come back clean, with all three 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity, and your hit points are full. The long rest ends at ten to five on Day 6, and the lamp by the shrine is still burning. Nobody woke you in the night.

You're 100 XP short of level 3. Mother Aldith is a few streets away, Perrin's hip and Wren's letter are still on your conscience, and the carter and the two children will need watching today. Under the second arch, the bridge is quiet.

What does Brannoc do?

I rise, wash at the basin, and cast Cure Wounds on Rudd's thigh and a gentle check over Imma and Tobin before I leave. Then I ask Brother Ansel to show me the way to Mother Aldith's house on the tanners' lane, and thank him for the bed.

At her door I'll introduce myself, hand her Wren's letter, and tell her about Perrin Gale's crooked hip in Greywater and Tobin's crushed ankle here, asking if she can see the boy today. DM: has Hodd's night watch at the grating seen or heard anything since I left?

input.add_to_description: Day 6 ~6:30 AM: Brannoc reaches her house on the tanners' lane. Wren kept her original letter, so Brannoc wrote a fresh note in his prayer book for Aldith.

transcript.result: added to Mother Aldith's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

You wash at the basin, then lay your hand over Rudd's splinted thigh and say the prayer low. Thirteen points of life go in. His colour comes up and the ache eases from his face. The bone still has to knit, and he'll be on a crutch for weeks. But he'll live, and he'll keep the leg. Imma sits up, hungry and cross, her head clear enough to complain about it. Tobin's ankle is still swollen and purple, and the gray finger-marks have faded to a bruise. He needs a bonesetter. You have two 1st-level slots left.

Ansel meets you at the green door with a heel of bread. The night was quiet, and he has the answer to your question. Hodd's watch saw nothing and heard nothing. One of the guards swore he heard water dripping on stone near midnight, but it didn't move, and no runner came. Ansel gives you directions with the bowl still in his hand. Down the tanners' lane, third door past the dye-pit, and look for the bone hung over the lintel. He'll send Tobin along on a litter once the boy has eaten.

A mistake of mine first. Wren kept the letter you gave her, and she held it too tightly to give back. So you tear a fresh leaf from your prayer book and write a new note by the shrine lamp. It's two lines: who you are, who sent you, and that a girl in Greywater wants to learn.

The tanners' lane stinks, and the morning is cold. The door is the one with the pale bone nailed above it. Before you can knock, a voice from inside bellows, "If you're bleeding, come in. If you're selling, go to the devil!"

Inside is a low, hot room with a table scarred by knives, a shelf of splints and rolled bandages, and a heavy woman of sixty with forearms like a smith's. She is up to her elbows in a bowl of flour and looks you over without stopping. "A priest. You've the look of Edda's. Well? Speak."

What does Brannoc say?

"Good morning, Mother Aldith. I'm Brannoc Ashdown, Edda Thorne's foster-son, and I've come with two matters. A boy named Tobin has a crushed ankle at Brother Ansel's hospice, and a dyer in Greywater, Perrin Gale, has a hip that healed crooked after a fall from a rack."

I hold out the note. "This is also from me, for a dyer's daughter named Wren, twelve, who sweeps the chapel there and wants to learn the work. Maud Marrow vouches for her, and her parents have agreed to a month's trial. Will you read it, and will you see Tobin today?"
dice Brannoc's Persuasion with blunt Mother Aldith, DC 12 (honest, mentions Maud and Edda): 1d20+2 = 1d20 [16] + 2 = 18

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: Agreed to see Tobin today at the hospice; will read the note on Wren and take her on a trial when she arrives with Maud. Told Brannoc to send Perrin Gale to her only if he comes himself; she won't travel to Greywater before the first frost. She asked Brannoc about the gray marks on Tobin's ankle.

transcript.result: added to Mother Aldith's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

Aldith wipes her hands on her apron, takes the note, and reads it standing, with her lips moving. Then she reads it again.

"Edda Thorne's boy." She grunts. "Taught me to pack a wound with moss when I was nineteen and a fool. Is she dead?" You tell her, and she nods slowly and says nothing for a breath. "She'd have hated a fuss. Good."

Persuasion (18): she asks what you want in plain words and you answer in plain words, and it counts. Maud's name helps most. "Maud Marrow's blankets are the only reason I've not frozen these ten winters. If she vouches for the girl, that's one thing, and if the girl can count breaths and keep her mouth shut, that's another. Send her down with Maud when the weather holds. A month. If she faints at the first bad break, she goes home. If she doesn't, we'll talk."

On Tobin, she's already pulling her bag off a hook. "Crushed? Then I'll see it before the swelling sets harder. I'll come now. Your priest can hold the lad's shoulders while I do it." She stops with her hand on the latch. "What are these marks Ansel's boy was babbling about, round the ankle?"

You tell her briefly. She says nothing, her jaw hard, and then shrugs her bag onto her shoulder.

On Perrin, she's flatter. "A hip healed crooked a month ago? I'd have to break it again, and he has to come to me. I'll not trek upvalley for a man too proud to ask. Tell him that, and tell him I said it kindly."

It's a quarter to seven on Day 6. Aldith is ready to leave for the hospice, and she is looking at you to see if you are coming.

What does Brannoc do?

"I'm coming, Mother Aldith. I'll hold Tobin's shoulders and hum to him while you work, and I'll carry your message to Perrin, kindly as you meant it."

On the walk I'll tell her what the marks looked like and where we sealed the Drowned Stair. DM: do I have a Healing Word ready if Tobin's pain from the setting becomes too much, and can I use one of my two slots on him afterward?

input.add_to_description: Day 6 ~7:30 AM: At the hospice she set Tobin's ankle; the first set did not quite seat (shy of right), and she grumbles it must be re-done after the swelling eases or the boy will limp. Brannoc told her about the Drowned Stair seal on the walk.

transcript.result: added to Mother Aldith's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Mother Aldith

On the walk you tell her all of it: the four gray finger-marks with the frost-burn at their tips, the forced padlock, the two ghouls at the grating, and the capstone and clay. Aldith listens with her bag bumping her hip and her face growing grimmer. "My grandmother called that the Stair-Wife's grip," she says. "Said she took boys who went down for the oil. I took it for a nursery tale." She spits. "I was a fool."

At the hospice she shoos Ansel and his apprentice back and kneels at Tobin's cot. You hold his shoulders and hum Edda's hymn low into his hair, and he clings to your sleeve with both hands. Aldith works fast, with her thumbs, her eyes shut, and her tongue between her teeth. The crack of bone comes once, and Tobin cries out. Then she binds the ankle in splints and wet linen, not gently.

Her Medicine roll is a 12, a hair short of what the crush needed. She sits back, wipes her brow, and frowns at her own work. "Near enough to hold, not near enough to be proud of. The bones are in the right country but not the right house. Give the swelling three days to go down and I'll reset it, or he'll limp for life. Better a second time than a crooked foot." She says it flatly, without apology, and you can hear that she is angry with herself.

Healing Word is ready, with two 1st-level slots left. It restores hit points as a bonus action and wouldn't straighten a bone, but it would ease his body's hurt now, and Tobin is a small boy who has just been through a bad quarter hour. It's your call, and it costs a slot you might want if the bridge wakes tonight.

It's about half past seven on Day 6. Aldith is packing her bag. Rudd is stable, Imma is cross and recovering, and Tobin sniffles against your sleeve. You're 100 XP short of level 3. Perrin's message still needs carrying, and the road goes on in both directions.

What does Brannoc do?

I cast Healing Word on Tobin to ease his hurt, since a nine-year-old who just had his bones set deserves a little mercy. I'm keeping my last slot for tonight.

"You were brave, Tobin. Mother Aldith will finish the job in three days, and I'll tell Rudd and Imma you didn't make a sound after the first." Then I tell Aldith, "I'll carry your message to Perrin kindly, and send Wren and Maud your way. I'll look in on the grating once more before I leave town."

You say the few words of the prayer, and eight points of life settle into Tobin. It doesn't touch the bone. The shaking goes out of him, though, and the grey pinch leaves his mouth. He lets go of your sleeve at last and gives you a wobbling, offended look. "I didn't cry," he says. "Not after." You solemnly agree, and promise to tell Rudd and Imma the same.

Aldith snorts at that and shoulders her bag. "Three days," she says. "I'll be back before the swelling goes. And tell the dyer, kindly, that if he comes himself I'll set him in half a morning. If I have to hear he sat on his stool and sulked, I'll send him the bill." That is as near to a blessing as you'll get from her. She nods to you and is out of the door, heading for the lane.

You take your leave of Ansel, who gives you a hard, warm hand and a word: come back, and bring a letter from Hollow Reach for the wall, since the shrine keeps a book of the faithful. Rudd, drowsy, mutters his thanks. Imma tries to give you her last honey-cake and is talked out of it.

Then you walk to the bridge in the thin morning, and the second arch is quiet. Hodd is there with a drawn face, sitting on an upturned crate with a lantern between his boots. Two guards, Bede and a new man, lean on the parapet. Bede lifts his halberd in a salute. The capstone and the clay are as you left them, and nothing has stirred since midnight. Hodd says he'll set the second stone today and wants a priest's blessing on it. A man scared of the dark is one thing, he says, but a man scared of the dark with a watch to keep is another.

It's twenty past eight on Day 6. You have one 1st-level slot, Channel Divinity, and 100 XP to go for level 3. The road north is a day to Greywater and beyond that the Reach, and the valley south of Stonebridge is yet unwalked.

What does Brannoc do?

I lay a hand on the capstone and speak a short blessing over it, asking that the stair stay shut and the light stay kept. Then I tell Hodd, "Light the niches every dusk, and send word to Brother Ansel if the scratching ever comes back."

"DM: with a day's walk north to Greywater and the Reach, would the road south be a better place to find the next village with no healer? I'd like to carry Aldith's message to Perrin first, so I think I'll head north and ask Maud about the way."

input.description: The valley south of Stonebridge is unwalked. Brannoc has not yet heard of a village without a healer there; Ansel or Captain Voss could point to one. Ghoul nests (Long Cut, Drowned Stair) hint at a connected barrow network, the Dead Road, running beneath the valley.

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Road south of Stonebridge; added 1 relationship to Road south of Stonebridge

You lay your palm on the cold capstone and say the blessing: that the stair stay shut, and the light stay kept. It is only words, and a man's hand on stone, and I'll not pretend it is more than that. Hodd takes off his hat for it all the same. He promises to light the niches every dusk and send word to Ansel at the first scratch. Bede grins and says he'll take the night watch himself.

Your question: the road south is an unknown. You have no word of a village there that wants a healer. Ansel or Captain Voss could tell you more if you asked, and it's worth asking before you go. Perrin and Wren are a certain errand, and the Reach is a day behind that. North is the sensible road.

So you walk north. The valley road takes you back past the toll-hut, the mill, and the bored keeper, who waves. The river runs broad on your right now. You've the loaf, the honey, and Hale's dried apples to eat as you go. By half past four the slate roofs of Greywater come up out of the afternoon haze, with the dye racks red and blue along the bank and the weir white and loud. The chapel door stands open. Someone has swept the step.

On the lane by the dye-sheds, Wren sees you first. She drops her yarn basket where she stands and runs.

It's half past four on Day 6. You have one 1st-level slot and Channel Divinity, 100 XP short of level 3. Perrin is in his dye-shed and Maud is at her loom. Wren is out of breath, with news plainly written on her face.

What does Brannoc do?

I crouch and catch Wren by the shoulders as she skids to a stop. "Easy, breathe. Tell me what's happened, and is everyone all right: Ilsa and Tessa, Osric, Perrin?"

Once I've heard her, I'll go straight where she leads me, and afterward pass along Mother Aldith's message to Perrin and tell her and Maud that the bonesetter will take Wren on a month's trial.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 afternoon: Has been using the stool at the vat and sleeping through the night since Brannoc's Cure Wounds; privately asking Wren what the priest meant about the bonesetter.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Perrin Gale
time: 20 minutes later: Day 6, 4:50:42 PM

You catch her by the shoulders. She's gasping with a grin that won't stay down, and the words come out all anyhow. "Nobody's hurt! Everybody's better! Tessa fed all night, and Ilsa slept, and Osric's red has gone back down the arm, and I changed the dressing twice!" She takes a breath. "And Perrin's been sitting on the stool for two days, and he asked me what you meant about the bonesetter. He didn't say he wanted to go. He only asked."

Then she lowers her voice, as if announcing a state secret. "And Garn the carter is at Maud's. The one from the Millstone. He says his boy is sitting up and eating an egg, and he wanted to find you."

She leads you down the lane at a half-run. First stop is the dye-shed. Perrin is sitting on the three-legged stool at his vat, scowling at the madder with his chin up. He doesn't greet you. He says to the vat, "Well?"

You give him Aldith's word kindly, as she meant it. She'll set the hip in half a morning if he comes himself, and she will not trek upvalley for a man too proud to ask. She'll have Wren on trial for a month, too, once Maud takes her down. Perrin's jaw works for a long while. "Proud," he mutters. "She's said it to my face before. Forty years back, over a broken wrist." A pause. "Kindly, you said she meant it?" You tell him yes. He gives a short grunt that might be a laugh. "Then I'll think on the walking. Down the valley, a day. On this." He slaps the hip, and his face tightens. But he does not say no.

Maud is at her door, shuttle in hand, with a broad man in a carter's coat bent awkwardly beside her. Garn has Piper's chin and a hat crushed in both fists. He thanks you in three clumsy words, Maud tells him to sit down before he falls down, and he presses a small leather purse into your hand. It holds three silver pieces. Maud, when Wren tells her about the month in Stonebridge, only says, "I'll go. I've a debt to the old tyrant anyway," and goes red about the ears.

It's ten to five on Day 6. You've delivered Aldith's word and Wren's news. You have three silver pieces more than you had and one 1st-level slot, with 100 XP to go to level 3. The chapel is swept, and Ilsa's lamp is lit down the lane.

What does Brannoc do?

I thank Garn and tell him to spend the silver on Piper, not on me: "Honey and good broth for the boy, and keep him upright when the cough returns." Then I walk down to Ilsa's house to count Tessa's breaths one more time and check Osric's arm, since I promised both.

After that I'll sit with Maud and Wren to plan the trip to Stonebridge, and tell Maud that Hob's sister is expected at the Lamp within the week. DM: Maud said she'd go up to Hob's lamp-house within the week, so has she settled when, and is there anything she'd want me to carry up ahead of her?
