input.add_to_description: Day 6 evening: Plans to take Wren to Stonebridge to Mother Aldith first (a week, when weather holds), then go up to the Lamp after the trip, a few days later than she said. Wants Brannoc to carry up her old loom-stool? No: she asks him to tell the Reach to expect her, and sends a skein of blue wool for Hob's lamp-house.

transcript.result: added to Maud Marrow's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Maud Marrow

Garn tries to press the silver on you twice more. You hold up both hands, and he finally mutters something about honey and broth and puts the purse away. He has the look of a man who will remember a debt for twenty years.

At Ilsa's house you count Tessa's breaths against a slow sixty in the window light. Medicine (15): they're easy and even, with no rattle left and a pink face. Ilsa has colour in her cheeks and says she slept through. Osric's arm, in the dye-shed, has closed along the split, and the red has gone back to the edge of the dressing. There are no streaks and no fever. Wren's linen is the cleanest you've seen. He nods at you, and says Wren is a hard woman to disobey.

You sit with Maud and Wren in the warm, crowded room. Maud says she'll take the girl down to Stonebridge in two days, once the loom order is done. They'll stay a few days with Aldith and see how the month starts. She'll go up to the Lamp after that, early next week. She will not be hurried, and she says so. She has two things for you to carry ahead. One is a skein of blue wool to hang in the lamp-house, "so he'll know someone's coming", and the other is a message for the Reach: expect a woman who talks too much.

It's half past six on Day 6. The light is going, you've kept your promises, and you have one 1st-level slot with Channel Divinity ready. You're 100 XP short of level 3. The road north goes back to Hollow Reach and the Lamp, a day and a half away. There is also the unwalked road south of Stonebridge. The chapel is yours for the night if you want it, and Ansel asked you to send a letter from the Reach.

What does Brannoc do?

I take the skein of blue wool and thank Maud. "I'll hang it in the lamp-house myself and tell Hob his sister is coming early next week. And I'll tell the Reach to expect a woman who talks too much."

I'll sleep in the chapel tonight, with Wren's sweeping to keep me company, and set out north at first light for Hollow Reach. DM: do I have enough rations and candles for the road, and are Pell and Dorrin likely to have started the Lamp watch yet?
sheet: gained 1 × Skein of blue wool (Maud's, for Hob's lamp-house)
time: 2 hours 20 minutes later: Day 6, 8:50:42 PM
sheet: long rest: HP, spell slots and features restored; hit dice regained; 8 hours later: Day 7, 4:50:42 AM

Maud wraps the skein in a scrap of cloth and presses it into your hands. "Blue. He'll know it." You promise to hang it in the lamp-house yourself, and to tell Hob that his sister is coming early next week, talking all the way.

Your question about supplies: you have two day-rations, the heel of Maud's loaf, Hale's dried apples, and the jar of honey. That's enough for a day and a half to the Reach if you eat plainly, and the Millstone Inn is on the road, where Hesper would feed you anyway. You have five candles, plus fifty flasks of lamp oil. The oil is far more than you need, so you could leave some at the Lamp. As for Pell and Dorrin, Berra Fenner promised oil weekly and the rota began on Day 4. By my reckoning it's running by now, but you won't know until you see the lamp-house with your own eyes.

You sleep in the chapel. Wren sweeps the floor around you until she is sent home, and sleep finds you quickly. Edda's hymn is still in your head. You wake at ten to five on Day 7, before dawn, with the stone cold under your pallet. Your hit points are full at 17, all three 1st-level slots are back, and Channel Divinity is ready. Your prepared list is Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary and Protection from Evil and Good, and you may change it now.

The lane is dark and still. Someone has left a bowl of porridge and a twist of blue wool by the altar again. You're 100 XP short of level 3.

Which prayers does Brannoc prepare, and does he set out now or wait for the sun?

I keep my list as it is: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready. It has served me well against the ghouls.

I eat Maud's porridge at the altar, tuck the blue skein and the five candles into my pack, and leave a note on the altar for Wren to keep sweeping. Then I set out north in the dark with a lantern, since the road is a known one, and walk steadily toward the Millstone Inn and Hollow Reach.
time: 8 hours 20 minutes later: Day 7, 1:10:42 PM

input.add_to_description: Day 7 ~1 PM: Brannoc returns to Hollow Reach carrying Maud's blue skein and her message (she comes up to the Lamp early next week). Tam meets him on the track. The rota has been running since Day 4.

transcript.result: added to Lamp Watch's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Lamp Watch

You eat Maud's porridge standing at the altar, leave your note for Wren under the jar of wildflowers, and set out in the dark with the lantern swinging. Dawn finds you on the valley road with mist on the river. You pass the Millstone Inn about seven. Hesper is at the pump and waves a ladle at you without stopping, and from the back window comes a thin, cheerful voice calling "Humming man!" You wave back and keep on. The day is clear and the road dry, and the Reach comes up out of the hills a little after one o'clock.

The lanterns on the porches are lit in the afternoon, which was Dorrin's doing, no doubt, and not one door is shut. The fences have been mended where the ghouls came through. Old Garrit sits on a stool by the well with a bad knee and his staff across his lap, and gives you a nod like a flag.

Tam sees you from the barn lane and comes running with his shirt untucked and his father's crutch banging behind him on the wall. He pulls up short, remembers himself, and says in a rush, "Pell's at the Lamp now! He took the oil Berra sent, and Dorrin goes up at dusk, and nothing's come up the track for three nights, nothing at all! Mam says the scratching at the slab has stopped." He swallows. "Are you staying? You said you'd think about it."

It's ten past one on Day 7. You have 800 XP, 100 short of level 3, and all three 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity ready. You carry Maud's skein and message, and Ansel's wish for a letter from the Reach. The Lamp is an hour north. Joss is mending in his house, and the barn is quiet.

What does Brannoc do?

I ruffle Tam's hair and smile. "I'm glad of that news, Tam. I'm not staying for good, but I'll be here a few days first. I've messages to carry."

I'll go up to the Lamp to hang Maud's blue skein, tell Pell and Hob that Maud is coming early next week, and see the lamp-house for myself. On the way back I'll look in on Joss, Wil and Widow Harrow, and ask Joss to write a short letter for Brother Ansel's book of the faithful.

DM: has Nessa Tarn gone up with the oil yet, and does the slab at the Long Cut still show any sign of cracking?
time: 1 hour 10 minutes later: Day 7, 2:20:42 PM
sheet: lost 1 × Skein of blue wool (Maud's, for Hob's lamp-house)

input.add_to_description: Day 7 ~2:30 PM: Brannoc hung Maud's blue skein in the lamp-house and told Hob she is coming early next week. Hob says, in the quiet of the night, he hears the crypt beneath the lamp is empty now; the ghouls have gone south along the Dead Road toward the river-town (Stonebridge). Two had already gone before the Drowned Stair fight.

transcript.result: added to Hob Marrow's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Hob Marrow

Tam grins so widely it must hurt. He answers your questions as you walk him to the lane's end. Nessa went up on the second day with Pell, he says, carrying a cup of oil in both hands like a child with a candle. She sat two hours and came back and told the whole street. As for the slab at the Long Cut, Garrit and Dobb's cousin went down to look at it yesterday. There are no new cracks, no frost on the stone, and the crack at the corner is still finger-wide. They've heard nothing from it in three days.

The track north is dry and dim under the beeches, and the lamp-house shows a gold smudge long before you reach it. The lamp is lit even by daylight, and the step is swept. Your five candles still stand there in a row, burned low and replaced with fresh ones. Pell sits on a stool by the door with a knife and a half-carved spoon. He's pale but steady, the arm moving easily now. He stands when he sees you, and for a moment he can't say anything. Then he says, "Dorrin said you'd come back." You tell him Maud is coming early next week, and he nods slowly and says he'll sweep for her.

Inside, Hob stands where the light falls on the floor, tall and gray and still. You tell him in your own words: Maud knows, she cried, she kept the shawl, she is coming up with a loom-stool, and she is going to talk the whole time. You hang the blue skein from a nail by the window where the lamp-light falls on it. Hob looks at it for a long while.

"Talks too much," he says at last, in his dry rasp, and something in the sound is not a rasp. "Good."

Then he turns his head toward the flagstone in the corner and is quiet. "The crypt is empty," he says. "Three nights now. They have gone." He lifts a gray hand and points, slow and certain, south and east, toward the river. "Down the long road under the hill. Not here. Somewhere there are hungry mouths and no light." That is all he knows. It matches the Drowned Stair.

It's twenty past two on Day 7. You've done what you came to do at the Lamp. You have all three slots and Channel Divinity, and you're 100 XP short of level 3. Joss, Wil and Widow Harrow are an hour's walk back at the Reach, and a letter for Ansel's book needs writing.

What does Brannoc do?

"Thank you, Hob. I'll carry that word too." I ask him gently, "Can you tell me anything more about the long road under the hill: where it surfaces, how many went down it, and whether any are still hurt like the one Cal's arrows and Corra's spears wounded?"

Then I'll leave a few flasks of oil from my fifty for Pell's watch, and tell him to send word to me through Brother Ansel if the stones ever stir. After that I'll walk back to the Reach, look in on Joss, Wil and Widow Harrow, and help Joss write his letter for Ansel's book.
sheet: lost 5 × Oil (flask); gained 1 × Letter from Hollow Reach for Brother Ansel's book of the faithful
time: 2 hours 40 minutes later: Day 7, 5:00:42 PM

input.add_to_description: Hob cannot count the ghouls or say where the Dead Road surfaces; he feels footfalls, not numbers. He senses one that moved slowly and dragged a leg (the wounded Ghoul 2, 3 HP). He wants a message sent through Ansel if the stones stir.

transcript.result: added to Hob Marrow's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Hob Marrow

Hob takes a long time to answer, as a man does who is counting things he can't see. "I do not count," he says at last. "I hear. Feet, and the drag of a heavy thing along stone. Many nights ago there were four I knew by their steps. One went quiet when the oil burned. One came back hurt, and went under the stone, and did not run again, but I heard it dragging a leg when the flagstone shifted. Since the Long Cut, that one has not come back." He looks toward the corner. "I cannot say where the road comes up. The way is long, and under the hill it forgets whose it is."

He lifts the lamp-house lantern gently from its hook, trims the wick with a gray thumb, and hangs it again. "Tell Maud the lamp was lit. And tell Pell I like his spoons."

You leave ten of your fifty flasks, no, five, on the shelf by the door for Pell's watch, and tell him to send word through Brother Ansel if the stones ever stir. He promises, then adds with a grin that he's never carved a better spoon.

The walk back is quiet. Joss is on his porch in the sun with his crutch beside him, and he gives you a crooked grin. Wil is up and loud, arguing with a goat, and you let yourself be glad of it. Widow Harrow sets a stool for you without a word and brings broth. At Joss's table you help him with the letter, which takes an hour. He writes slowly in a farmer's careful hand, and you add the dates. Hollow Reach asks the house of the healing faith to keep a place in its book for Cal Tarn, Marl, Hennet, Dobb, Wat and Ned, who died keeping the dark out. He signs it with Tam's name beside his own. It goes in your pack for Ansel.

It's five o'clock on Day 7. You've seen the Lamp and spoken to Hob, and checked on Joss, Wil and Widow Harrow. The letter is written. Your slots are full and your Channel Divinity is ready, and you're 100 XP short of level 3. The ghouls have gone south, along a road under the hill, toward Stonebridge, and you've already met two of them there.

What does Brannoc do?

I tuck Joss's letter safely into my pack and thank him and Widow Harrow for the broth. "I'll stay the night in the barn with Tam and rest, then head back south at first light. Hob says the hungry ones have gone down the long road under the hill, and Stonebridge and the Drowned Stair are where I've seen them."

Before I go, I'll ask Joss and Garrit if anyone knows where a burial hill or old barrow lies between here and Stonebridge, since that road must come up somewhere. DM: do I remember the Dead Road Hodd mentioned under the Drowned Stair, the one running toward the burial hill outside Stonebridge's walls?
time: 3 hours 50 minutes later: Day 7, 8:50:42 PM
sheet: long rest: HP, spell slots and features restored; hit dice regained; 8 hours later: Day 8, 4:50:42 AM

input.description: Old Garrit's name (his grandmother's tale) for a string of old barrow mounds along the valley, said to be joined by one long road under the hills: the Dead Road. Known or suspected links: the Wayfarers' Lamp crypt, the Long Cut, the burial hill outside Stonebridge's walls, and the Drowned Stair vault. Garrit says there were seven; he can name only the Long Cut and the Lamp, and has heard that one lies on the hill above Stonebridge and another near the old ruined chapel on the valley road between the Millstone Inn and Greywater.
relationships: connected beneath the valley by the Dead Road
includes [[The Long Cut]], [[Wayfarers' Lamp]] and [[The Drowned Stair]]

transcript.result: entry The Sleepers' Chain (legend) created; relationship [50] added to The Sleepers' Chain; relationship [51] added to The Sleepers' Chain

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for The Sleepers' Chain; added 2 relationships to The Sleepers' Chain

Yes, you remember the Dead Road. At the bridge, Hodd said the old tale spoke of a sealed passage running from the vault under the Drowned Stair toward the burial hill outside Stonebridge's walls. He had never seen it. It is the only road you know of that fits what Hob heard, though Hob couldn't say where it surfaces.

Joss and Garrit are glad of the question, and they argue it for an hour over a jug of small beer. Garrit's grandmother had a name for it: the Sleepers' Chain, seven mounds on seven hills, joined by a road under the ground that no living foot was meant to walk. He can name only two, the Long Cut and the Lamp, and he has heard of two more but never seen them. One is the burial hill above Stonebridge, and the other is somewhere near the old ruined chapel on the valley road between the Millstone Inn and Greywater, the one with the fallen roof. That would be the one you passed on Day 4, past the ford. He says it as an old man's tale, and he says he is sorry now that he never believed it.

You spend the night in the barn, the same barn that held the wounded a week ago. Tam sits beside your pallet until his mother calls him, and he doesn't ask again if you're staying. He only says, "Come back and see the lamp in the spring," and you say you will. Your prayers return with the long rest. You wake on Day 8 at ten to five, with all your slots, Channel Divinity, and your hit points full, and the lantern on the barn porch is still lit.

The road to Stonebridge is two days on foot, by way of the Millstone Inn and Greywater, eight hours to Greywater and another eight to the bridge. You carry Joss's letter, and you are 100 XP from level 3. Four of the seven mounds are known to you now, and the nearest unvisited one may be the ruined chapel on the road, a few hours short of Greywater.

Do you change your prepared prayers, and what does Brannoc do?

I keep my prepared prayers as they are, since Protection from Evil and Good is exactly what I want if more ghouls rise. I take my leave of Tam, Joss, and the Harrows, shoulder my pack, and set out south at first light.

I'll stop at the Millstone Inn for the night and check on Piper, then look hard at the ruined chapel past the ford in daylight, from a distance, before deciding whether to go in. DM: how many candles and flasks of oil do I have left after leaving some at the Lamp?
time: 6 hours 40 minutes later: Day 8, 11:30:42 AM

input.add_to_description: Day 8 ~11:30 AM: sitting up, eating, nearly well; has a weak cough. Calls Brannoc the humming man.

transcript.result: added to Piper's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Piper

You still have five candles and forty-five flasks of oil. You left five flasks at the Lamp, as you meant to. The candles are the five that were left over from Day 3, and Pell's watch has its own.

You say your goodbyes in the cold before dawn. Tam hugs you round the middle, hard, and says nothing at all. Joss lifts his crutch in salute. Widow Harrow is at her door with her arms crossed and gives you a single nod, which from her is a benediction. Then the track is yours, the lantern swings, and the beeches thin out into fields. You walk south for six hours with the sun coming up gold on the right.

At about half past eleven, the Millstone Inn comes into view with its wheel turning in the stream. Hesper is at the door with her sleeves rolled, and she sees you before you speak. "The humming man," she says dryly. "Bed and board's still yours, and so is a boy who won't stop talking about you."

Piper is propped on cushions in the back room with a bowl of eggs on his knees and colour in his face. His cough is only a small dry one now. He wants to know about the road and the Lamp and whether you are really a priest, and whether priests can fight. You tell him a priest mostly sits and hums. He gives you a long look and says he doesn't believe it. Hesper confirms the sickness has not come back. It's been three days, no blue on his lips, and Garn took him a week's care of honey and broth and is off to Greywater again with his cart.

It's half past eleven on Day 8. The ruined chapel past the ford is about an hour south of the inn, an hour short of Greywater, on the road you walked on Day 4, and the afternoon is long and bright. You have all your slots, Channel Divinity, and 100 XP to go for level 3. You could eat, rest here, and go in the morning, or walk down now and look at the chapel from a distance in good light.

What does Brannoc do?

I eat Hesper's stew and sit a few minutes with Piper. "Keep the honey water coming and the eggs too, and no running until the cough is gone a full week." Then I thank Hesper and walk down in the bright afternoon to look at the ruined chapel from a distance.

I'll stop at the ford and study the roofless walls, the ground around the door, and any signs of missing lamps or gray handprints before going near. DM: from the ford, can I see anything unusual, like scorched earth, fresh tracks, or an open crypt door?
dice Brannoc's Perception studying the ruined chapel from the ford, DC 13: 1d20+3 = 1d20 [6] + 3 = 9
time: 1 hour 45 minutes later: Day 8, 1:15:42 PM

input.description: Roofless old chapel on the valley road about an hour south of the Millstone Inn, just past a ford. Behind it, hidden by brambles, is a low barrow mound, one of the Sleepers' Chain. Hidden truth: a fallen altar-slab inside covers a stair to a crypt, and the slab has been shifted a hand's width from below; faint gray finger-marks on its underside edge and a few gnawed sheep bones in the nettles by the east wall. The wounded ghoul (Ghoul 2) has not yet come this far. Brannoc failed to spot these from the ford (Perception 9).
relationships: on the road between [[The Millstone Inn]] and [[Greywater]]

transcript.result: entry Ruined chapel at the ford (place) created; relationship [52] added to Ruined chapel at the ford; relationship [53] added to Ruined chapel at the ford

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Ruined chapel at the ford; added 2 relationships to Ruined chapel at the ford

You tell Piper to keep up the honey water and the eggs, and no running until the cough has been gone a full week. He grumbles that a week is a very long time, and Hesper says it's what a week is for. You thank her, and she sends you off with a pasty wrapped in cloth. The stew was as good as ever.

The road south is bright and dry, and the afternoon is warm. A little after one you reach the ford. The river is low and clear over brown stones. You stop on the near bank, under an alder, and study the ruin from across the water.

Perception (9): it's an old chapel, roofless, with three walls and part of a fourth standing, the gable end black with age. Nettles and brambles crowd it. A stone doorway has no door. You can make out nothing out of the ordinary from where you are. No scorching, no tracks you can read at this distance, no open crypt door. The ground round the walls is thick with weeds, and the daylight lies flat on everything. It doesn't say it's safe. It just doesn't say anything. If there is something to see, you'd have to go closer.

It's a quarter past one on Day 8. You have all your slots, Channel Divinity, Protection from Evil and Good and its powder, forty-five flasks of oil, and the road to Greywater a short walk beyond. The light is good for another six hours. You could cross and look properly, in daylight, with care. You could light your way on, or go back and ask Hesper whether anyone has seen anything strange on the road. The ford is knee-deep and easy.

What does Brannoc do?

I cross the ford slowly, shield on my arm, and approach the chapel in the good light, stopping at the doorway to look and listen before I step in. I'll look for a flagstone or stair that has been moved, any missing lamps or old oil flasks, and gray finger-marks on the stone, and I'll keep a flask of oil and my lantern ready to light.

If I find a sealed crypt, I won't open it alone. I'll mark the place, and bring Greywater's folk and some oil to seal it properly, as we did at the Long Cut.
dice Brannoc's Perception searching the chapel doorway and floor up close in good light, DC 12: 1d20+3 = 1d20 [14] + 3 = 17
time: 25 minutes later: Day 8, 1:40:42 PM

input.add_to_description: Day 8 ~1:40 PM: Brannoc searched up close (Perception 17) and found the shifted altar-slab, the finger-marks and the gnawed bones. He chose not to open it alone; plans to bring Greywater folk and oil to seal it.

transcript.result: added to Ruined chapel at the ford's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Ruined chapel at the ford

You wade the ford slowly, with the water cold round your knees and your shield on your arm. On the far bank you stop and listen. There's the river, a wood-pigeon, and the wind in the nettles, and nothing else. You go up to the doorway with a flask in your hand and your lantern at your belt, and you look before you step in.

Perception (17): the floor is flagstone under a skin of moss and rubble, the altar a long slab at the east end, toppled at one corner. Under the nettles by the east wall lie a few bones, a sheep's, gnawed and scattered, and not by a fox. Then you see the slab. It has been moved. A hand's width of black gap shows along its near edge, as if it had been pushed from below, and on the underside of the lip, where the dust is thin, are four long gray smears like finger-marks, spread wide. The air coming up out of the gap is cold and smells of grave-earth. You hear nothing from below.

You don't open it, as you decided. You tie a strip of your linen to a bramble at the doorway to mark the place, then back out the way you came. You note the bones, the slab, and the position of the ruin: an hour south of the Millstone Inn, an hour short of Greywater, with a barrow mound hidden behind the brambles at its back. You've found your fifth mound.

It's twenty to two on Day 8. You have all your slots and Channel Divinity, and forty-five flasks of oil. Greywater is an hour on, with a chapel, a dyer's family who owe you no debt but a good will, and Maud, who knows most of the valley. Hesper is an hour behind. The slab won't wait for ever, though no sign of anything stirring has come up since you arrived.

What does Brannoc do?

I head on to Greywater to raise help rather than seal it alone. "Maud knows this valley, and Osric and Corwin will have hands, ropes and a cart. I'll ask for a few strong volunteers, the capstone-and-clay method we used at the bridge, and a few of my flasks of oil, and we'll come back at first light."

I'll also ask Maud if she knows any tale of this chapel. DM: since I'm 100 XP short of level 3, would helping seal this barrow count as a milestone worth the XP?
time: 1 hour 15 minutes later: Day 8, 2:55:42 PM

input.add_to_description: Day 8 ~3 PM: Told Brannoc the ruined chapel at the ford was the Ford Chapel, abandoned after the Grey Fever years ago; shepherds say sheep vanish near it, and her grandmother called its mound the Sleepers' Hill. She offers her cart-owning cousin and a fortnight's worth of lamp oil from the dye-sheds.

transcript.result: added to Maud Marrow's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Maud Marrow

On XP: yes. When the Reach sealed the Long Cut, I gave you 100 XP for it. Sealing a barrow mouth with a threat behind it, at real risk, is the same kind of challenge. I'd rule it worth at least 100, which is exactly what takes you to 900 and level 3. If it goes badly, with a fight at the slab, ghouls count by the book on top of that.

You reach Greywater a little before three, with the dye racks red and gold in the afternoon light. You go straight to Maud's blue door. She is at her loom, hears you out without a word, and stops the shuttle. "The Ford Chapel," she says. "Sleepers' Hill, my grandmother called the mound behind it. Shut up after the Grey Fever, when there was no one left to ring the bell. Shepherds don't graze that bank. They lose ewes there and blame foxes." She wipes her hands. "My cousin Tobias has a cart and a mule. I'll send him. And the dye-sheds have lamp oil to spare."

Within the hour you have your help. Corwin comes without being asked, with a coil of rope and a crowbar the length of his arm. Osric brings his good hand and his stubbornness. Tobias arrives with the cart and a young apprentice named Fenn, and Wren hovers at the edge of everything with a face like a fist. She is told she is not coming, and she nods with her jaw set. Corwin says dryly she may bring the lamp.

The plan is yours: capstone-and-clay, as at the bridge, oil poured and lit, wedges, and the slab dragged back into its seat with the cart-mule, at first light. You have forty-five flasks, and the village adds a dozen more.

It's five to three on Day 8. You can't take a full rest until tomorrow morning, because your last one ended at ten to five today. Your slots are full and your Channel Divinity is ready, and you have the afternoon and night in Greywater.

What does Brannoc do?

I thank Maud, Corwin, Osric and Tobias, and ask everyone to rest and eat well tonight so we start fresh at first light. "Nobody goes near that slab alone, and nobody goes down. If anything stirs, we drop the tools and pull back to the cart."

Tonight I'll check Ilsa, Tessa and Osric's arm one last time, then sleep in the chapel with Wren's sweeping for company. DM: can Wren and Maud be on their way to Stonebridge before we go, or will they wait until the barrow is sealed?
time: 5 hours 55 minutes later: Day 8, 8:50:42 PM
sheet: long rest: HP, spell slots and features restored; hit dice regained; 8 hours later: Day 9, 4:50:42 AM

Your question about the trip: Stonebridge lies south of Greywater, and the Ford Chapel lies north, so Maud and Wren aren't going past it either way. Maud says they'll wait a day and leave once the slab is dealt with. "I'll not have that girl on the road while there's a mound open behind me," she says, and Wren, who is pretending not to listen, goes quiet and pleased. They'll set out in the afternoon after you're back.

The evening goes as you planned. Tessa sleeps easy on her mother's shoulder when you count her breaths, and Ilsa has been up and about all day and is cross to be told to sit. Osric's arm has closed well, and he holds it out for you to see like a man showing a fish. You eat at Corwin's table, where nobody talks about the slab, and everyone says early nights. Nobody goes near the chapel but you. Wren sweeps around your pallet until Hale comes to fetch her.

You wake at ten to five on Day 9 with all your prayers, Channel Divinity, and 17 hit points. Your prepared list is Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good. As your character goes on adventures and overcomes challenges, he or she gains experience, represented by experience points. A character who reaches a specified experience point total advances in capability. This advancement is called gaining a level.

When your character gains a level, his or her class often grants additional features, as detailed in the class description. Some of these features allow you to increase your ability scores, either increasing two scores by 1 each or increasing one score by 2. You can't increase an ability score above 20. The slab won't go back cleanly on the first try. Corwin and Osric drag at it with the crowbar and the mule hauls, but the edge catches on a lip of stone, and it is a finger's breadth short of its seat. Tobias swears at the mule and the mule swears back. It takes an hour of cutting a new oak wedge, shifting the capstone, and packing clay, but the second try seats it tight. You pour oil along the seam and light it for good measure, and it burns clean and steady. Nothing stirs below, not once, in all that time. You hold your hand to the stone afterward. It is cold, and still, and sound.

It is ten to nine on Day 9. The sealing is done. For overcoming a barrow mouth in the Sleepers' Chain, I've given you 100 XP, so you now stand at 900. That is level 3, and it's yours to take.

Here is what the level gives. All the choices are yours.

Hit points: take the fixed 5 (plus your Constitution +2, so 7 more hit points, for a maximum of 24), or roll a d8 and add 2 (at least 1 in all cases).

Spell slots: four 1st-level slots and two 2nd-level slots.

New always-prepared spells: Lesser Restoration and Spiritual Weapon. They are domain spells and don't count against your list. Lesser Restoration would have broken Piper's fever, and ends paralysis from a ghoul's claws. Spiritual Weapon is a bonus-action spell.

You may now prepare six spells from the whole cleric list after your next long rest, up from five. You can change them then.

Preserve Life now restores 15 hit points, divided among those you choose.

How would you like to take your hit points, fixed or rolled?

I'll take the fixed 7 again. Brannoc has learned not to trust the dice, and Lesser Restoration is what I've wanted since Piper's fever and the ghoul's claws.

For my sixth prepared spell after the next long rest, I'll keep Protection from Evil and Good and add Command, since it works on the living. Then I'll thank Corwin, Osric and Tobias and ride back to Greywater on the cart to tell Wren and Maud it's sealed.

You're now a cleric of the third level, and the sheet is updated. Your maximum is 24 hit points, and the seven you took came on top of the old seventeen, so you're at 24 of 24. You have four 1st-level slots and two 2nd-level slots, and the new always-prepared spells are Lesser Restoration and Spiritual Weapon. Preserve Life now heals 15 hit points. Your hit dice are 3 of 3.

On the list: you can prepare six spells after your next long rest, which can't be before ten to five tomorrow morning. Command is on the cleric list and works on the living, so you can take it. Keep Protection from Evil and Good, and you'd have Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, Protection from Evil and Good, and Command.

You thank Corwin, Osric and Tobias in turn. Corwin wipes his hands on his apron and says the first thing he's said to you all morning that isn't about rope: "Edda's boy. She'd have been proud." Osric nods at the slab. Tobias gives you a place on the cart-bed beside the oil, and the mule plods back toward Greywater.

You arrive at half past ten. The racks of dyed wool are bright in the sun. Wren is waiting on the chapel step with her basket, and she runs to the cart before it stops. You tell her everything, as you promised, and she listens with her mouth shut tight. At the end she says, "So it's done," and you say yes, for now. Maud comes up the lane, wiping her hands, to hear it. She says she'll pack the loom-stool and a blanket, and they can leave for Stonebridge within the hour if you'll walk with them as far as the first milestone.

It's half past ten on Day 9. You have your new slots, Channel Divinity, and a letter for Brother Ansel. Wren and Maud are ready to go, Perrin is on his stool at the vat, and the road to Stonebridge is a day's walk.

What does Brannoc do?

I'll walk with Maud and Wren, and I'll ask Perrin to come along with us to Stonebridge. "Master Perrin, Mother Aldith said she'd set your hip in half a morning if you came yourself. Maud's cart is going the same road, so you wouldn't be walking alone."

On the way I'll carry Wren's pack and teach her the Healing Word prayer's first line. I'll also deliver Joss's letter to Brother Ansel and check on Tobin's ankle. DM: does Maud's cousin Tobias have room on his cart for Perrin so he doesn't have to walk that hip a day?

Perrin is on his stool at the vat when you come, scowling at the madder. You say it plainly and kindly, as Aldith meant it. Persuasion (20): he is quiet a long while, then looks at Wren, who is trying very hard not to look at him. "Fifty-one years I've dyed," he says to the vat. "I'll not die on a stool." He stands, slaps the hip, and tells Hale to mind the sheds. Tobias has room. He lays sacks and a blanket in the cart-bed, and Perrin climbs in with a great deal of muttering.

The road south is slow with the cart, but the day is dry and bright. You carry Wren's pack beside your own. She walks at your elbow and asks about everything. You teach her the first line of the hymn that goes with Healing Word, the plain words only. They are a prayer, not a spell, and she can't cast from them. She says them anyway, three times, under her breath, until she has them right. Maud talks the whole way, as promised: dyes, weather, Hob as a boy, and Aldith's temper. Perrin pretends to sleep and listens to every word.

You pass the toll-hut and the mill. The river runs on your left, and the seven arches of Stonebridge come up out of the dusk at a quarter to eight. Lanterns are lit along the parapet, and Hodd's niche-lamps glow under the second arch. It all looks quiet. At the gate, the tired guardsman looks at the cart, the bone-setter's patient and the weaver, and waves you through with a grunt.

It's a quarter to eight on Day 9. You have all your slots and Channel Divinity, at 24 of 24 hit points. Joss's letter is for Brother Ansel, whose hospice is past the tannery. Tobin is there, and Mother Aldith's house on the tanners' lane is a few streets on.

What does Brannoc do?

I guide the cart through the gate toward the tanners' lane first. "Mother Aldith, I've brought you Perrin Gale, Maud Marrow, and Wren, the girl from my letter. Perrin's hip is the one I told you of, and he came on his own two stubborn feet, nearly."

Once they're settled, I'll go to the hospice, hand Joss's letter to Brother Ansel for the book of the faithful, and look in on Tobin's ankle, Rudd and Imma. DM: has Hodd or Captain Voss seen anything at the Drowned Stair since I left?

You steer the cart down the tanners' lane to the door with the bone over the lintel. Aldith opens it before you knock, flour to the elbows again, and looks at the cart like a woman inspecting a sack of grain. "Perrin Gale," she says. "Forty years and you've still not learned to ask." Perrin says something short and rude. She says "Good," and nearly smiles.

She looks Wren over once, from braid to boots. "You're the counter of breaths. Can you hold a lamp steady?" Wren says yes, sir, then no, ma'am, and Aldith says either will do. Maud puts down her loom-stool with a thump and begins to talk. Aldith tells her to sit. They will all stay under her roof, and she will look at the hip at dawn, not by candlelight, as she says "I'm not a fool." You help Perrin down from the cart, and he leans on your arm harder than he'd ever admit.

Insight (16): Aldith's grumbling is real, but under it she is glad. She isn't hiding anything from you. As for the Stair, Aldith says she went to the hospice at noon and reset Tobin's ankle herself, and it sat right the second time. And Captain Voss's men have walked the bridge twice a day. Hodd's lamps have burned every dusk, and nothing has scratched. Only one thing nags at her. Hodd told the guard that the water under the second arch has been running oddly cold for two nights, and a mist has hung there at dawn.

At the hospice, Ansel takes Joss's letter in both hands and reads it standing under the shrine lamp. He says nothing for a while. Then he opens the book of the faithful on the lectern and writes the six names in his own hand, one by one, with the date. Tobin's ankle is splinted and set straight, and he is awake and boasting. Rudd is sitting up with a crutch, and Imma has been sent home with a headache and strict orders.

It's a quarter past nine on Day 9. You have all your slots and Channel Divinity. The cold water under the arch troubles you, and the bridge is two streets away. Ansel offers you your old cot.

What does Brannoc do?

Before I sleep, I'll walk to the bridge with a lantern and a few flasks of oil to see the second arch for myself. "Brother Ansel, thank you for writing their names. I'll be back within the hour, and I'll sleep on my old cot after."

At the arch I'll look from the parapet, not go down. I'll check the capstone, the clay and the grating for new marks, and ask Hodd about the cold mist. DM: are the niche-lamps still burning, and does the water or the mist look different tonight than when we sealed it?

input.add_to_description: Day 9 night: grating, capstone and clay intact, second stone set by Hodd. But the river under the second arch runs unnaturally cold, with a low mist, and a faint scrape of stone is heard from the vault side, not the stair: the drain culvert toward the river is the likely new route. Something is moving in the vault below (a third ghoul, probably the wounded Ghoul 2 or another arrived by the Dead Road).

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Drowned Stair

You take your lantern and three flasks, tell Ansel you'll be back within the hour, and walk the two streets to the bridge. The night is cold and clear, with the river loud beneath the arches.

Hodd is on his crate by the parapet with a blanket over his knees, and he stands when he sees you. All the niche-lamps under the second and third arches are lit. Hodd climbed down to trim them himself an hour ago. The new capstone sits on the old one, with clay packed round it, and the grating is as you left it. Perception (18): there are no new marks on the stone, no fresh gray fingers, and nothing scratching on the stair.

But the water is wrong. Under the second arch, the river runs black and still, and a low white mist lies on it, thick as milk, though the night is clear everywhere else. It doesn't drift with the current. The air off it is cold enough to bite. And from somewhere under the stone, not from the stair but farther along toward the bank, you catch a slow, wet scrape, like something heavy being dragged through shallows. It stops when you hold your breath. Hodd says he's heard it for two nights and told the captain. She sent a man to look at the culvert, who found nothing but the bars intact.

The grated drain from the vault opens to the river a little downstream, too small for a man. It's wide enough for something that crawls.

It's close to ten at night on Day 9. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and forty-five flasks of oil. Ansel's cot is two streets away, and your prayers can't be refreshed until the morning.

What does Brannoc do?

"Hodd, thank you. Stay up here and keep the lamps lit. Nobody goes down to the water."

I'll walk along the bank to the drain culvert with my lantern, shield up and two guards if Captain Voss can spare them, and look at it from above without climbing in. If something is crawling out of that grate, I'd rather meet it with Corra and Bede, a shield of faith on me, and oil ready to burn.

DM: where is the culvert's outlet, and can I reach a spot on the bank above it that gives a clear view and a clear line to throw oil?

input.add_to_description: Day 9 ~10:20 PM: The culvert outlet is a stone-lipped arch-mouth in the quay wall on the east bank, about forty paces downstream of the second arch, a hand's height above the low water, grated with iron bars two fingers apart. A flat bank ledge ten feet above it gives a clear line down. Brannoc brings Corra and Bede.

transcript.result: added to The Drowned Stair's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Drowned Stair

Hodd stays on his crate and says he'll keep every lamp lit if he has to feed them his own coat. Captain Voss is still in the guardhouse, and she hears you out over a cold mug without comment. Then she sends for Corra and Bede, who both come at a trot. Bede grins as if you were old friends, and Corra gives the lantern a long look. "Not going down, then?" she asks. You tell her no.

The culvert's outlet lies on the east bank, forty paces downstream of the second arch. It's a stone-lipped arch-mouth in the quay wall, a hand's height above the low water, closed with iron bars two fingers apart. There's a flat ledge on the quay about ten feet above it, with a low rail, where the watch tie up boats. From there you have a clear view straight down onto the grate and a clear line to throw. The mist lies here as well, in a thin cold skin on the water, and the lantern light turns it a sickly yellow.

You set your shield, and your companions set their spears. Nothing moves. The drag you heard comes again from the dark behind the bars, nearer now, slow and wet. Then it stops. In the silence a long gray hand slides out between the bars, fingers spread wide, and rests on the stone lip as if feeling for warmth. It is blistered black along the back, and there's a spear-wound in the wrist that has never closed.

You know that hand. Hob said it dragged a leg.

It's twenty past ten on Day 9, and the ghoul is below you in the dark. It hasn't seen you yet. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and a flask of oil in your hand. Corra and Bede stand either side of you.

What does Brannoc do?

I whisper, "That's the wounded one Hob heard. Corra, Bede, hold still and stay clear of the bars." I cast Shield of Faith on myself, then hurl a flask of oil at the grate and light it, so the fire keeps it pinned behind the iron.

If it stays hurt and frightened, I'll finish it with Sacred Flame from here, out of reach, and save my 2nd-level slots for Lesser Restoration if any of us gets clawed.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Drowned Stair

You whisper for Corra and Bede to hold still, and they do. You call on the shield of faith, a shimmer round you like a held breath (AC 20). Then you tip the lantern flame to a rag stuffed in the neck of a flask and hurl it, a ruling of mine, that lighting it costs you a free hand's work.

The throw is a 7, short of the bars, and the flask bursts on the stone lip. Oil runs over the quay and through the iron, and fire goes up bright and yellow across the mouth of the culvert. The gray hand snatches back into the dark. The wrenching at the bars you heard a breath earlier stops. A thin, furious hiss comes from the tunnel, then a drag of limbs, going away fast. It is running back up the culvert, away from the light.

The oil burns for two rounds and gutters out. The grate is whole, the bars unbent, and the mist on the water thins and drifts. Behind the iron, the culvert is black and silent. Nobody is hurt, and the ghoul is not dead, only hurt and frightened, and now it knows this way is watched.

It's about twenty-five past ten on Day 9. Shield of Faith still holds you for ten minutes. You have three 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and forty-four flasks. The culvert leads back to the vault, and the vault to the Dead Road, and the burial hill outside the walls is the mound you have not seen.

What does Brannoc do?

"Bede, Corra, thank you for holding steady. Captain Voss should know that this one's down to a few hit points and afraid of fire."

I'll ask Bede to fetch an iron-banded plate or a second grate and a keg of oil from the quay yard, and I'll pour a line of oil along the culvert mouth to light if it returns. Then I'll walk up to the burial hill outside the walls at first light with Voss's guards, to find where the Dead Road surfaces.

'Concentration' is a heading inside the rules section Duration; the whole section:

RULE Duration:
A spell's duration is the length of time the spell persists. A duration can be expressed in rounds, minutes, hours, or even years. Some spells specify that their effects last until the spells are dispelled or destroyed.

#### Instantaneous

Many spells are instantaneous. The spell harms, heals, creates, or alters a creature or an object in a way that can't be dispelled, because its magic exists only for an instant.

#### Concentration

Some spells require you to maintain concentration in order to keep their magic active. If you lose concentration, such a spell ends.

If a spell must be maintained with concentration, that fact appears in its Duration entry, and the spell specifies how long you can concentrate on it. You can end concentration at any time (no action required).

Normal activity, such as moving and attacking, doesn't interfere with concentration. The following factors can break concentration:
- **Casting another spell that requires concentration.** You lose concentration on a spell if you cast another spell that requires concentration. You can't concentrate on two spells at once.
- **Taking damage.** Whenever you take damage while you are concentrating on a spell, you must make a Constitution saving throw to maintain your concentration. The DC equals 10 or half the damage you take, whichever number is higher. If you take damage from multiple sources, such as an arrow and a dragon's breath, you make a separate saving throw for each source of damage.
- **Being incapacitated or killed.** You lose concentration on a spell if you are incapacitated or if you die.

The GM might also decide that certain environmental phenomena, such as a wave crashing over you while you're on a storm-tossed ship, require you to succeed on a DC 10 Constitution saving throw to maintain concentration on a spell.

SPELL Command: level 1 enchantment
Casting time 1 action; range 60 feet; components V; duration 1 round
Classes: Cleric, Paladin
You speak a one-word command to a creature you can see within range. The target must succeed on a wisdom saving throw or follow the command on its next turn. The spell has no effect if the target is undead, if it doesn't understand your language, or if your command is directly harmful to it.
Some typical commands and their effects follow. You might issue a command other than one described here. If you do so, the GM determines how the target behaves. If the target can't follow your command, the spell ends.
***Approach.*** The target moves toward you by the shortest and most direct route, ending its turn if it moves within 5 feet of you.
***Drop.*** The target drops whatever it is holding and then ends its turn.
***Flee.*** The target spends its turn moving away from you by the fastest available means.
***Grovel.*** The target falls prone and then ends its turn.
***Halt.*** The target doesn't move and takes no actions. A flying creature stays aloft, provided that it is able to do so. If it must move to stay aloft, it flies the minimum distance needed to remain in the air.
At higher levels: When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 2nd level or higher, you can affect one additional creature for each slot level above 1st. The creatures must be within 30 feet of each other when you target them.

input.description: Grassy burial hill outside the north wall of Stonebridge, an old barrow, one of the Sleepers' Chain, used for the town's plague dead during the Grey Fever, hence unvisited. Captain Voss's grandmother called it Stair-Wife's Hill. On the east flank, behind an overgrown stone kerb, a low door-slab has been shoved ajar a forearm's width from within; fresh drag-marks run to the culvert side of the hill. The Dead Road reaches the surface here.
relationships: reached by the Dead Road from [[The Drowned Stair]]

Daylight first: it's the middle of autumn, so about nine hours of good light remain, with dusk at roughly half past five. You've time to look, but not to dawdle.

On the walk Voss answers the second question without slowing her limp. The hill is the old plague-ground, she says, where the town buried its dead in the Grey Fever years, and no one has used it since. Her grandmother called it Stair-Wife's Hill and told the children to stay off it after dark. "I thought it was to keep us from the drop-off by the quarry," she says, flatly.

The hill is a long green swell north of the wall, with rooks on the crown and a low kerb of tumbled stone round its foot. You walk the base slowly with the three of them behind you, and you leave no stone unlooked at.

Perception (15): on the east flank, half hidden in nettles behind the kerb, is a low door-slab set into the hillside. It stands ajar by about a forearm's width, pushed out from within. The earth in front of it is scuffed and trampled, and long drag-marks run through the grass, downhill toward the town and the river, in the line of the culvert. There are old gray finger-smears on the slab's inner edge. Cold air breathes out of the gap and the smell of grave-earth with it. No oil-flasks, no lamps. You hear a slow, dry sound inside, like something shifting on loose stone.

Voss has gone very still. "That's no tale, then." Her hand rests on her sword hilt.

It's a quarter to nine on Day 10. You have four 1st-level and two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, Protection from Evil and Good with its powder, and thirty-eight flasks of oil. Corra holds a rope, and Bede has a halberd. The door is ajar, and the sun is full on the hillside.

What does Brannoc do?

I hold up a hand to keep everyone back from the door. "Nobody step in front of that gap. Bede and Corra, stand to either side with spears ready, and Captain, keep the rope tied off at the oak behind us so we can haul anyone out."

I'll pour oil across the threshold and light it to keep whatever is inside from coming out into the sun, and cast Protection from Evil and Good on whoever stands closest to the door. If it's the one hurt ghoul alone, we hold the door with fire and Sacred Flame; if it's more, we seal it with the capstone-and-clay method, with no one going in.

Behind the fire, the ghoul does not run and does not charge. It crouches a pace inside the slab, pale eyes fixed on the flames, gray hands flexing on the dirt. I cast Sacred Flame at the crouching ghoul through the fire, since it has only 3 hit points and the radiance ignores cover. "Corra, Bede, hold your ground. If it dies, we seal the door as planned."

If it somehow survives, I'll ask it quietly to surrender its hunger, and fight on with my mace only if it comes through the flames.

Sacred Flame falls through the fire onto the crouching ghoul, and it fails to dodge. It hisses as the radiance scorches it, but it is only a spark of what it needs to be. It still lives, a hand's breadth from death, with the flames in front of it.

Then Bede's halberd comes in over the fire, a hard clean thrust, and takes it through the chest. It makes no sound. The pale eyes go dark, and the thing slumps against the slab. The flames gutter and go out on the stone. I let your concentration on the protection lapse, since the threat is over.

For the last ghoul, you earn 200 XP, and you now have 1,100 of the 2,700 needed for level 4. Voss lets out a long breath behind you. "That's the one, then?" You tell her it's the one Hob heard, the last of the band you know of. Hob counted four, and you've seen four fall.

You and the guards haul the slab shut and pack it with clay and stone from the kerb, as you did before. Nothing stirs inside. Voss says she'll have the watch bring a capstone from the quay yard and set it by noon. Then she looks at the hill and then at you, and says that Stonebridge owes you a debt, and a captain remembers.

It's ten to nine on Day 10. You have three 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and thirty-seven flasks. Perrin's hip is being seen to, Wren is learning, and Ansel's book has its six names. The road south of Stonebridge is unwalked, and nothing else holds you here.

What does Brannoc do?

I help Bede and Corra finish packing the slab, then thank Captain Voss. "No debt, Captain. Just keep the niche-lamps lit and the watch walking the bridge, and send word to Brother Ansel if anything stirs."

I'll go back to Aldith's to see Perrin's hip set and say goodbye to Wren and Maud, then to Ansel to hand over the rest of the news. After that I'll set out south on the unwalked road, looking for the next village with no healer. DM: do I still have Hob's message for Maud, and what's my coin total now?

You help Bede and Corra pack the last clay into the slab. Voss grips your forearm hard and says you owe nothing and the town owes you plenty, and that she'll remember it, which from her is the sort of word that gets kept. She promises the niche-lamps and the watch. A runner will go to Ansel at any scratch.

To your questions: you no longer carry Hob's message for Maud. You delivered all of it on Day 4, and the skein and the news about the lamp went to her and to Hob since. The one small thing left is the last word Hob gave you for her, "tell Maud the lamp was lit," which you passed on in Greywater when you told her. You also hold no one else's errand. Your coin is 10 gold. Garn's three silver went back into his own purse when you refused it, so your sheet is right.

At Aldith's you hold Perrin's shoulders while she works. It's slow and brutal, and the old dyer says several things about her mother. Aldith's Medicine check is a 10, short of the 14 the hip needed. She sets it well, but not perfectly. The joint sits seated and the high shoulder is level, but the leg is still half an inch short, and she tells him so flatly. "You'll walk with a stick, and without the grinding. In a month it'll be better than it's been in a year. In a year, come back and I'll look again, and don't come back late." Perrin, white and sweating, says it's the first time in a month he could feel his foot. He cries a little and says it's the sweat.

Wren is on a stool by the bed with a lamp held steady all the morning, as Aldith ordered. Maud has made the old tyrant a cup of tea and a speech. The goodbyes are quick and warm. Wren hugs your middle, hard, and says "Yes, Brannoc" when you tell her to count breaths. Ansel gets his news at the hospice and blesses the road.

Before you leave, Captain Voss, who walked with you, gives you one more thing: Reedholm. It is a fen village two days south on the river road, reed-cutters and eel-trappers, with a marsh-fever and no healer since old Mother Vane died in spring. The carters speak of lights seen over a drowned barrow in the reeds, but carters will say anything.

It's a quarter past one on Day 10. You have three 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and thirty-seven flasks of oil. You could leave now for Reedholm, or rest in Stonebridge tonight and set out fresh in the morning.

What does Brannoc do?

I'll rest at Ansel's hospice tonight so my prayers are full, and set out for Reedholm at first light. Before I go I'll buy rope, a second lantern, and a few more candles from the market with my 10 gp, and check on Tobin and Rudd one last time.

"Captain Voss, if anyone south of here has seen those lights over the drowned barrow, I'd like to know before I go." DM: is a marsh-fever something Lesser Restoration could cure, and what should I ask the carters about the road to Reedholm?

Your first question: yes, probably. Lesser Restoration touches a creature and ends one disease or one of four conditions: blinded, deafened, paralyzed, or poisoned. A marsh-fever is a disease, and it would end it. But it ends one disease on one creature per casting, and you have only two 2nd-level slots a day. If the whole village is sick, you can't cast your way through it. You'd have to use your Medicine to find who is worst off and who simply needs rest, water and a clean bed. It wouldn't touch what the fever left behind, such as weakness or a ruined lung.

You spend the afternoon and evening on errands. At the market you buy fifty feet of hempen rope (1 gp), a hooded lantern (5 gp, burns six hours on a flask, and you can lower the hood to dim it), and five more candles. That's 6 gp, and you're left with 4. Tobin shows you his ankle and asks about the hill. Rudd is up on his crutch complaining about the porridge. You sit with Imma's father at the cart-yard for a while, and ask the carters what you meant to.

You learn this. The river road south forks at a wooden milestone, the Eel Fork. The east branch goes to Reedholm along a causeway, two days on foot, with a ferry-rope at the Black Ford, which a boy keeps. The lights over the drowned barrow are pale green-white and seen on moonless nights, and the reed-cutters call them the Wick-fires. A boy named Sedge brought the first fever cases to market last week and went home sick. Voss, when you ask her, has nothing more. Nobody on her watch has been south of the Eel Fork this month.

You sleep late, from nearly midnight, under the shrine lamp. The long rest ends at twenty to eight on Day 11. You wake with 24 of 24 hit points, four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity ready. Your prepared list is unchanged. You have thirty-seven flasks, two lanterns, rope, ten candles, and 4 gp. The morning is clear, and Ansel stands at the green door with a heel of bread and a twist of dried willow-bark for fever.

What does Brannoc do?

I thank Ansel, take the bread and the willow-bark, and bless the hospice door before I go. "Keep the book open for Reedholm's names, Brother. I'll write if I can."

Then I set out south on the river road toward the Eel Fork, keeping a steady pace and an eye on the reeds. DM: the carters said Sedge, the boy with the fever, went home sick, so is he the first person I should ask for when I reach Reedholm?

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Sedge; added 1 relationship to Sedge

Yes, Sedge is a good first name to ask for. He is the boy who carried the fever to market, so whoever tends him will know how it began, and the first sick are often the best clue to how a sickness spreads. He is about thirteen, a Reedholm eel-boy, and the carters could tell you nothing more of him. You've never met him.

You bless the hospice door with a thumb of ash from the shrine lamp, and Ansel says he will keep the book open. The willow-bark goes in your pack, a bitter, useful thing for a fever. The road south is flat and good at first, then rougher as the valley widens into low water-meadows. The day is cold and clear, with geese in the sky. You walk nine hours with a rest at noon, and the Eel Fork comes up a little after five: a wooden milestone at the split, with a worn carving of an eel, and the east branch dropping away onto a raised causeway between flooded fields.

The light is going amber. Ahead the road runs out over black water and reeds, the reeds waist-high and hissing in the wind. There is a shepherd's hut a hundred paces off the road, empty, with its roof sound and a hearth. Beyond the reeds, far off, a mist is rising.

It's ten past five on Day 11, with Reedholm about a day and a half on. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and thirty-seven flasks. Night is a couple of hours off, and the moon is a thin sliver.

What does Brannoc do?

I take the east branch onto the causeway and walk on a little way, then turn back to the shepherd's hut before dark. "Better a dry hearth tonight than the reeds at night with a thin moon."

I'll check the hut for anything unwelcome first, light a small fire, and keep a lantern hooded by the door. DM: from the hut, can I see the mist or any green-white lights over the reeds once it's dark?

input.description: Empty shepherd's hut a hundred paces off the Eel Fork, roof sound, hearth working. Hidden: a sweat-stained pallet pushed under the bench where a fever-sick traveller (a Reedholm woman, Marta Quill, trying to reach Stonebridge) rested days ago and moved on or collapsed in the reeds; Brannoc's Perception 7 missed it. Faint green-white glimmer low over the reeds at night, unclear to him (Perception 11).
relationships: near the Eel Fork on the road to [[Reedholm]]

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Shepherd's hut at the Eel Fork; added 1 relationship to Shepherd's hut at the Eel Fork

You walk on a little way along the causeway, with black water either side and the reeds hissing, and then think better of it and turn back. A dry hearth is wiser than a night in the reeds under a thin moon.

The shepherd's hut is low and stout. You push open the door with the mace in your hand, and look it over with some care. You find a bench, a hearth, a hook for a lantern, a stack of dry reed-bundles, and a roof that doesn't leak. Perception (7): it seems empty and safe. You didn't look into the corners as carefully as you might have, since the light was fading and you were tired.

You light a small fire with the tinderbox and hood your new lantern by the door. You eat Ansel's bread and some of Hale's apples and warm your hands. Dark falls by seven. From the doorway at about eight you watch the reeds. A mist lies on the water, thick and low. Perception (11): there may be a pale, greenish glimmer far out low over the reeds, or it may be the glow of your own eyes after the fire. You cannot swear to it. It does not move. The wind drops. A heron calls once and is quiet.

It's eleven minutes past eight on Day 11. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and a fire that will last till midnight. You can't complete a long rest before ten to eight tomorrow morning.

What does Brannoc do?

I bar the door, bank the fire low, and sit up the first watch with my mace and shield beside me, humming softly and keeping the hooded lantern at hand. I'll sleep in my armor after midnight, with a flask of oil and the rope within reach.

If the pale glimmer comes nearer or moves, I'll wake at once and look for it from the doorway. DM: does the hut have a second door or window, and can I see the causeway from where I sit?
time: 2 hours 5 minutes later: Day 11, 10:16:06 PM

input.description: Reed-cutter's wife of about thirty from Reedholm, fever-sick, who set out two nights ago to reach Stonebridge for a healer for her small son Dab (left with kin). Staggers up the causeway with a failing lantern around 10:15 PM Day 11 and reaches the hut. Has the marsh-fever (hot, shivering, delirious in bursts). Carries news: the Wick-fires started when the reeds were cut near the drowned barrow, and the sick are those who cut reeds there.
relationships: seeks a healer; related to [[Sedge]] (her nephew)

transcript.result: entry Marta Quill (person) created; relationship [60] added to Marta Quill; relationship [61] added to Marta Quill

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Marta Quill; added 2 relationships to Marta Quill

The hut has one door, which you bar, and one small shuttered window beside it that looks out along the causeway. If you ease the shutter back a finger's width, you can see the pale ribbon of the road running out into the dark. You sit by the banked fire with your mace and shield at your side, the lantern hooded at your boot, and hum Edda's hymn under your breath. The glimmer over the reeds does not come nearer. It doesn't move at all.

At about a quarter past ten, something does. A small, wavering yellow light comes up the causeway out of the dark, a lantern held low and unsteady. It stops, and goes on, and stops again. Behind it, you can make out a shape bent double, walking like someone who has been walking too long. A cough carries on the still air, wet and deep. Then a woman's voice, thin and cracked, calling to nobody: "Please. Is it a house? Please."

She is alone as far as you can tell. The lantern is nearly out. She is about forty paces off and coming straight for the hut.

It's a quarter past ten on Day 11. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and your door barred. Your shield is by your hand.

What does Brannoc do?

I unbar the door, keeping my mace in my left hand and my shield on my arm, and step into the doorway with the hooded lantern opened a little. "Over here, goodwife, the door's open. I'm Brannoc, a healer. Come to the fire and sit, and don't try to talk yet."

Before she crosses the threshold I'll look her over: her lips and eyes for blue or yellow, her hands, and whether she walks like someone sick or something else, since I'm wary after the Drowned Stair. DM: does she cast a shadow and do her lips show any frost-burn like the gray marks on Tobin's ankle?
dice Brannoc's Medicine looking over Marta Quill at the door, DC 12: 1d20+5 = 1d20 [14] + 5 = 19

input.add_to_description: Day 11 ~10:30 PM: Reached the hut and was looked over by Brannoc (Medicine 19). Living, casts a shadow, no frost-burn. Marsh-fever: hot, shivering, dry cough, cracked lips, a rash of small red spots at the wrists, dark urine; a true disease. Her fever is high but she is lucid enough to speak. Her pallet was under the bench of the hut from two nights ago (she slept here once, then went on to Stonebridge, was turned back at the ford by a flooded stretch and returned).

transcript.result: added to Marta Quill's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Marta Quill

You unbar the door and step into the doorway with your shield on your arm, the mace in your left hand, and the hooded lantern opened a hand's width. "Over here, goodwife. I'm Brannoc, a healer. Come to the fire, and don't try to talk yet."

She stumbles into the light, and you look her over before she crosses the sill. Medicine (19): she is a woman of about thirty, reed-thin, in a stained wool cloak. Your lantern throws her shadow long and wavering across the threshold, and it's an honest living shadow. Her lips are cracked and dry, not blue and not frost-burned. Her hands are shaking, hot to the eye, and there is a rash of small red spots at both wrists. The whites of her eyes are clear, not yellow. Her breath is shallow and quick, her pulse hammers, and the cough she carries is a dry, hard one. She is walking like the sick, with that careful deliberate step, not like the dead. There is no sour grave-smell on her. She smells of reed-smoke and sweat.

This is a living woman with the marsh-fever, and a bad case.

You get her to the fire and onto the bench with the blanket round her shoulders. She gives her name between coughs: Marta Quill, a reed-cutter's wife from Reedholm. She set out two nights ago to reach Stonebridge for a healer for her little son Dab, and was turned back at a flooded stretch of the causeway, so she's been trying to get home. She slept in this hut once before, she says, under the bench, on the way out. She tells you about the lights. "They began when the reeds were cut by the old mound. The ones who cut there are the ones who sicken. Sedge was the first. My sister's boy."

It's twenty-six minutes to eleven on Day 11. She is hot and weak but lucid, and she needs help now. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, the willow-bark, and Lesser Restoration.

What does Brannoc do?

I sit beside her and take her wrist. "Marta, you're safe now. I can end this fever with a prayer, but first sip this: I'll steep Ansel's willow-bark in warm water for the heat."

Then I cast Lesser Restoration on her, using a 2nd-level slot, and keep the other for tomorrow. Once she can breathe easily, I'll ask her more about the old mound and who cut the reeds there, and whether Dab is sick too. DM: how many people in Reedholm have the fever, as far as she knows?

input.add_to_description: Day 11 night, from Marta Quill: about sixty folk; some fifteen sick, three dead (old Hobb Sallow, a baby, and a reed-cutter named Tam Rush). The sick are those who cut reeds at the Hollow Isle, a low drowned barrow in the fen cut for thatch two weeks ago after the autumn gale stripped roofs. Dab (Marta's son, age five) has a mild fever and is with her sister Wenna. The village is run by Headwoman Ode Rush; no one has tried to cross to the Isle since the Wick-fires appeared.

input.add_to_description: Day 11 ~midnight: Cured of the fever by Lesser Restoration (2nd-level slot). Weak, hungry, thankful. Plans to return with Brannoc. Sister: Wenna; son: Dab.

transcript.result: added to Marta Quill's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Marta Quill

You sit beside her and take her wrist. "Marta, you're safe now." You steep a pinch of Ansel's willow-bark in warm water over the fire, and she sips it gratefully, grimacing at the bitterness. Then you lay your hand on her burning forehead, say the prayer of Lesser Restoration, and spend one of your 2nd-level slots. The warmth gathers and goes in. It takes a heartbeat, and then her shaking stops. The spots at her wrists begin to fade, and the heat goes out of her skin like a tide going out. She draws a long, easy breath, the first in days, and begins to cry quietly.

The cure ends the disease, but not the weakness it left behind. She is still thin and worn, and she needs food and sleep. You give her bread and honey and a cup of broth made from your ration, and she eats like a famished child, and then she sleeps.

She wakes a little before midnight, clear-eyed, and tells you what she can. As far as she knows, about fifteen in Reedholm are sick, out of perhaps sixty. Three are dead: old Hobb Sallow, a baby, and a reed-cutter named Tam Rush. The sick are those who cut reeds at the Hollow Isle, a low drowned barrow in the fen where they cut thatch two weeks ago after the autumn gale stripped the roofs. The Wick-fires began that week. Her son Dab is five, with a mild fever, and he is with her sister Wenna. The headwoman, Ode Rush, will not let anyone cross to the Isle again.

It's just after midnight on Day 12. You have four 1st-level slots, one 2nd-level slot, and Channel Divinity, and you can't finish a long rest until a quarter to eight at the earliest. Marta sleeps by the fire. The glimmer over the reeds is still out there.

What does Brannoc do?

I tuck the blanket higher around Marta, bank the fire, and keep the watch while she sleeps, humming low. "Rest, Marta. At first light we walk to Reedholm together, slowly, and I'll see Dab and Wenna first."

I'll sleep a few hours after midnight with the door barred. DM: you mentioned the Hollow Isle is a drowned barrow, and the sick are the ones who cut reeds there. Does that match the Sleepers' Chain Garrit described, the seventh mound?

input.add_to_description: Day 12: the Hollow Isle (a drowned barrow in the fen near Reedholm, where reed-cutters fell sick) may be another link; Garrit said seven mounds. Brannoc now knows: Wayfarers' Lamp, Long Cut, Ford Chapel, Stonebridge burial hill (and the Drowned Stair vault). Hollow Isle would be a fifth mound; two more unknown.

transcript.result: added to The Sleepers' Chain's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Sleepers' Chain

It could be. Garrit said there were seven mounds in the Sleepers' Chain, and you have set foot at four: the Lamp, the Long Cut, the Ford Chapel, and the burial hill above Stonebridge, besides the vault under the Drowned Stair. A drowned barrow in the fen where the dead are buried under water would fit the old tale well. But you can't be sure from Marta's account alone. Garrit named only two of the seven and heard of two more, so whether the Hollow Isle is one of them, or whether the fever has some other cause, you'll know only when you see it.

You tuck the blanket higher round Marta, bank the fire, and keep the watch humming low, the glimmer still on the horizon. When you've watched your fill you lie down by the door with your armour on and the rope and a flask within reach, and sleep, a light sleep, the sleep of a man who half listens. Nothing comes. Nothing stirs on the causeway.

The long rest ends at a quarter past eight on Day 12. You wake with 24 of 24 hit points, four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. You may change your prepared prayers now, if you wish.

Marta is awake already, sitting up with the blanket round her, hollow-eyed and clear. The fever has not come back. She has eaten the last of the bread, and she tells you she can walk. The morning is grey and cold, and a thin mist lies on the reeds. Reedholm is a day and a half on.

Which prayers does Brannoc prepare, and how does he set out?

I'll swap Command for Detect Poison and Disease, since this is a fever village and I want to know what's in the water and the reeds. The rest stays: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good.

We set out slowly along the causeway, Marta on my arm with the blanket round her and the rope and lanterns at my belt. I'll share my last bread and apples as we go, keep a steady pace, and watch the reeds for any green-white glimmer.
